items.stem: Across an ideal 23 V rail in a rail-signalling relay-coil meter check, a 350 Ω resistor sits in series with a 600 Ω resistor whose p.d. is monitored by a parallel 1800 Ω non-ideal voltmeter.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains R_p = 450 Ω.
Adds 350 Ω to R_p and divides 23 V by R_tot.
Obtains I = 0.0288 A.
Multiplies supply current by R_p (or uses loaded divider ratio).
Obtains V_meter = 12.9 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the combined resistance of the 600 Ω resistor and the 1800 Ω voltmeter in parallel.
Calculate the current drawn from the DC supply while the voltmeter is connected.
Determine the potential difference displayed by the non-ideal voltmeter.

items.stem: Why must high-precision tolerance resistors be selected in matched pairs ($R_1$ and $R_{\mathrm{f}}$) when building a four-resistor difference amplifier?
items.workedSolution: Only when both branches share the exact ratio $R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$ does $V_{\mathrm{out}} = (V_+ - V_-)R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$ hold: resistor ratios on inverting and non-inverting paths must match so common-mode signals produce zero output.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that resistor ratios on inverting and non-inverting paths must match so common-mode signals produce zero output.

options.label: A
options.text: Resistor ratios on inverting and non-inverting paths must match so common-mode signals produce zero output.

options.label: B
options.text: Mismatched resistors reverse the power-supply polarity of the op-amp.
options.distractorRationale: Resistor tolerances do not change power-supply polarity.

options.label: C
options.text: Matched resistors are required solely to prevent the op-amp from overheating.
options.distractorRationale: Op-amp feedback resistors carry microamp/milliamp currents with tiny dissipation.

options.label: D
options.text: Matched resistors force the open-loop gain to equal unity.
options.distractorRationale: Open-loop gain is an internal IC property unaffected by external resistors.

items.stem: An ideal 8 V DC supply powers a greenhouse louver motor array with two parallel paths, as shown: one path holds 15 Ω and 18 Ω resistors in series, while the second holds a 13 Ω resistor. What current is registered by the ideal ammeter A?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 15 + 18 = 33 Ω, so I_1 = 8 / 33 = 0.242 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 8 / 13 = 0.615 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 0.858 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 0.242 A and 0.615 A to obtain 0.858 A.

items.stem: A plasma-chamber glow-wire shunt circuit connects a uniform cupronickel wire R_1 (length 4.5 m, area 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) in parallel with a 23 Ω shunt resistor, in series with a 7 Ω resistor across an ideal 16 V DC supply.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 2.85 Ω and combines in parallel with 23 Ω.
Obtains R_p = 2.54 Ω.
Adds 7 Ω to R_p and uses I = V / R_tot.
Obtains I_tot = 1.68 A.
Finds V_p and uses P_1 = V_p² / R_1.
Obtains P_1 = 6.35 W.

items.stem: The circuit diagram shows a field-calibration DC loop with two ideal cells of negligible internal resistance. Component values are ε₁ = 14.5 V, R₁ = 5.50 Ω, R₂ = 6.50 Ω, and R₃ = 3.50 Ω. The steady current in the bottom branch is measured as I₃ = 0.950 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Based on conservation of electric charge. (b) I₁ = 0.6937 A ≈ 0.694 A, so I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = 1.644 A ≈ 1.64 A. (c) ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 14.01 V ≈ 14.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: States conservation of electric charge.
Substitutes I₂ = I₁ + I₃ into ε₁ = I₁R₁ + I₂R₂ correctly.
Correct current I₁ = 0.694 A (and I₂ = 1.64 A).
Correctly evaluates middle-branch current I₂ = I₁ + I₃ and states ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Substitutes I₂R₂ and I₃R₃ consistently into the lower-loop equation.
Correct electromotive force ε₂ = 14.0 V.

parts.prompt: State the fundamental conservation law on which Kirchhoff's first law is based.
parts.expectedAnswer: Kirchhoff's first law is based on the conservation of electric charge.
workingSteps: Current entering a junction equals current leaving because charge cannot accumulate.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's laws to the upper loop and junction Q to calculate the current I₁ in the upper branch (and hence find I₂).
workingSteps: At junction Q: I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = I₁ + 0.950 A.
Middle branch: I₂ = 0.6937 A + 0.9500 A = 1.644 A ≈ 1.64 A.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's second law to the lower loop to determine the electromotive force ε₂.
workingSteps: State lower-loop equation: ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Calculate potential drop across R₂: I₂R₂ = 1.644 A × 6.5 = 10.68 V.
Add potential drop across R₃: ε₂ = 10.68 V + 3.325 V = 14.01 V ≈ 14.0 V.

items.stem: The diagram shows a non-inverting op-amp stage built with $R_1 = 6.00 kΩ$ and $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 114 kΩ$. The op-amp has saturation rails $\pm 14.0 V$ and a gain–bandwidth product of 1.80 MHz. An input signal of $+450 mV$ is applied.
items.workedSolution: (a) $G = 20.0$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 9.00 V$. (c) Max unsaturated input $= 700 mV$. (d) Bandwidth $= \mathrm{GBP}/|G| = 90.0 kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $G = 1 + R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$.
Obtains $G = 20.0$.
Computes $G V_{\mathrm{in}}$ and checks against $\pm V_{\mathrm{sat}}$.
Obtains $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 9.00 V$.
Applies $V_{\mathrm{in,max}} = V_{\mathrm{sat}}/|G|$.
Obtains 700 mV.
Applies $\mathrm{BW} = \mathrm{GBP}/|G|$.
Obtains 90.0 kHz.

items.stem: An N-channel enhancement MOSFET drives a $60.0\text{ }\Omega$ drain load resistor connected to a $15.0\text{ V}$ supply. At gate–source voltage $V_{\text{GS}} = 6.40\text{ V}$ (above $V_{\text{th}} = 2.40\text{ V}$), the drain current read from its characteristic curve is $I_{\text{D}} = 150\text{ mA}$. Calculate the drain–source voltage $V_{\text{DS}}$.
items.workedSolution: Load resistor drop $= I_{\text{D}} R_{\text{L}} = 0.150 \times 60.0 = 9.00\text{ V}$. Therefore $V_{\text{DS}} = 15.0 - 9.00 = 6.00 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 6.00 V.

items.workedSolution: (a) $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 350 ms$. (b) $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 210 ms$. (c) $\mathrm{PRF} = 1/(t_{\mathrm{H}} + t_{\mathrm{L}}) = 1.79 Hz$. (d) Mark-to-space ratio $= 1.67$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$.
Obtains 350 ms.
Uses $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$.
Obtains 210 ms.
Sums $T = t_{\mathrm{H}} + t_{\mathrm{L}}$ in seconds and takes $1/T$.
Obtains 1.79 Hz.
Mark-to-space ratio $= 1.67$.

items.stem: In the bench comparator circuit shown, two ideal cells of electromotive forces ε₁ = 2.00 V and ε₂ = 6.00 V are connected in opposition in series with R₁ = 2.00 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. An ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 2.50 V. What is the resistance of R₂?
items.workedSolution: Since the positive terminals face each other, net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.000 V. Current I = V₁ / R₁ = 1.250 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across R₂ is V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.500 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 1.200 × 10³ Ω ≈ 1.20 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses opposing net emf ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.00 V to find R₂ = 1.20 × 10³ Ω.

options.label: A
options.text: A data-logger eliminates the exponential nature of discharge so V falls linearly with time.
options.distractorRationale: The physics remains exponential V = V₀ e^(−t/RC); a data-logger simply captures accurate timestamps.

options.label: B
options.text: A data-logger records simultaneous (t, V) readings at high sample rate without human reaction-time lag; students still observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

options.label: C
options.text: A data-logger eliminates the need to check the capacitor's maximum working voltage rating.
options.distractorRationale: Exceeding the voltage rating damages the dielectric regardless of measurement instrument.

options.label: D
options.text: A data-logger draws a large bias current to stabilise the discharge curve.
options.distractorRationale: Voltage sensors must have very high input impedance so negligible current bypasses R.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a railway level-crossing beacon dimmer: an LDR whose resistance changes between 161 kΩ (dark) and 0.8 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 20 kΩ resistor across 9 V (ideal). What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 161 + 20 = 181 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 181000 = 4.97 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.994 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 20 / (0.8 + 20) = 8.65 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.994 V.

items.workedSolution: (a) R_p = 6.00 Ω, R_tot = 15.5 Ω, I = 1.40 A. (b) P_source = ε I = 30.4 W. (c) V_term = 18.2 V, so E_ext = V_term I t = 2.55 × 10³ J.

Applies P_source = ε I.

Obtains E_ext = 2.55 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Refer to the diagram for a tensile load-cell wire divider: series elements 5 Ω and platinum-iridium wire R_1 (L = 5.2 m, A = 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) are energised at 27 V (ideal). What is the potential difference across the platinum-iridium wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m)(5.2) / (6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 2.00 Ω. Series current I = 27 / (5 + 2.00) = 3.86 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 7.71 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 2.00 Ω and obtains 7.71 V.

items.stem: While bench-testing a balloon telemetry heater loop, an engineer wires a 18 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 14 Ω and 35 Ω resistors across an ideal 33.6 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 14 Ω and 35 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (14 × 35)/(14 + 35) = 10.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 33.6 × 10.0 / (18 + 10.0) = 12.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 10.0 Ω and finds V_p = 12.0 V.

items.stem: In the telemetry receiver circuit shown, two identical ideal cells of emf 9.00 V are wired in parallel across a 12.0 Ω resistor with an ideal ammeter A and voltmeter V.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = ε = 9.00 V, so I = ε / R = 0.750 A. (b) identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current.

markScheme.criterion: Correct ammeter reading 0.750 A.
States that identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current.

parts.prompt: Calculate the reading on the ammeter A.
workingSteps: For identical cells in parallel, V = ε = 9.00 V.

parts.prompt: Explain why connecting identical cells in parallel does not double the voltmeter reading.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current, the potential difference across both branches remains equal to the electromotive force of a single cell.
workingSteps: Each charge passes through only one cell on any closed loop, so parallel cells share current rather than adding energy per coulomb.

items.stem: At the marked operating point $(9.00\text{ V}, 0.750\text{ A})$ on the filament lamp $I\text{–}V$ graph, the tangent to the curve has slope $0.0476\text{ A V}^{-1}$. Calculate the electrical resistance of the filament at this operating point.
items.workedSolution: On any $I\text{–}V$ curve, resistance is strictly $R = V/I = 9.00 / 0.750 = 12.0 Ω$ (never $1/\text{gradient}$). Option A (12.0 Ω) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Operating-point resistance $R = V/I = 12.0 Ω$ (12.0 Ω, option A).

items.stem: A parallel LC tuned circuit ($L = 320\text{ }\mu\text{H}$, $C = 140\text{ pF}$) has a quality factor $Q = 62.0$. Calculate its half-power bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ in kHz.
items.workedSolution: $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{320 \times 10^{-6} \times 140 \times 10^{-12}}} = 752 kHz$. Using $Q = \frac{f_0}{f_{\mathrm{B}}}$, $f_{\mathrm{B}} = \frac{f_0}{Q} = 12.1 kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Half-power bandwidth equals 12.1 kHz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies $f_0$ by $Q$ instead of dividing $f_0 / Q$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the calculated bandwidth.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Erroneously multiplies bandwidth $f_0/Q$ by $0.707$.

items.stem: A battery of emf 117 V and internal resistance 3 Ω powers a mobile blood-bank compressor DC loop made of a 6 Ω series resistor and parallel 45 Ω and 90 Ω branches, as shown. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 50 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (45 × 90)/(45 + 90) = 30.0 Ω, R_ext = 6 + 30.0 = 36.0 Ω, and R_tot = 36.0 + 3 = 39.0 Ω. Current I = 117 / 39.0 = 3.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 117 − (3.00)(3) = 108 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 1.62 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 108 V.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a bench dry-cell assembly. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.600 A, V₁ = 8.10 V) and (I₂ = 1.80 A, V₂ = 6.30 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.500 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 9.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 30.0 mV when it carries 3.00 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 3.00 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 1.500 Ω ≈ 1.50 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 9.000 V ≈ 9.00 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01000 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.800 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.80 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0600 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 1.50 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 9.00 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0100 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.80 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0600 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 8.1 + 0.6 × 1.500 Ω = 9.000 V ≈ 9.00 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.03000 V / 3.000 A = 0.01000 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: In a light-gate receiver connected across a 12.0 V supply, a reverse-biased photodiode in series with a 125 kΩ resistor conducts a photocurrent of 60.0 μA. Calculate the potential difference remaining across the photodiode.
items.workedSolution: $V_R = (60.0 \times 10^{-6})(125 \times 10^3) = 7.50\text{ V}$. Hence the pd across the photodiode is $V_{\mathrm{D}} = 12.0 - 7.50 = 4.50 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Potential difference across photodiode equals 4.50 V.

Divides V_NTC by the series current from (a).
Obtains R_1 = 500 Ω.
Uses P = V I or I² R_1.
Obtains P = 8.00 × 10⁻³ W.

items.stem: Element R_1 in the autoclave seal heating-wire loop schematic is a cylindrical platinum-iridium wire (resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) of length 1.5 m and circular diameter 0.34 mm connected to an ideal 12 V cell. What steady current passes through R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.34 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 9.08 × 10⁻⁸ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 4.13 Ω. Current I = 12 / 4.13 = 2.91 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 34.9 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 2.91 A.

items.stem: In Required Practical 6, why does the voltmeter reading drop linearly as the variable resistance is decreased, and what precaution keeps the line straight?
items.workedSolution: RP6 mark-scheme explanation: Larger current increases lost volts Ir inside the cell so V = ε − Ir falls linearly; students must include a protective series resistor and open the switch between readings to avoid heating the cell so internal resistance stays constant.

options.label: C

items.stem: A series divider in a high-impedance sensor divider jig has a 100 Ω upper arm and 900 Ω lower arm across an ideal 36 V source. Connecting a non-ideal 1800 Ω voltmeter across the 900 Ω arm (forming the parallel pair shown) yields what potential difference?
items.workedSolution: The 1800 Ω voltmeter shunts the 900 Ω resistor: R_p = (900 × 1800)/(900 + 1800) = 600 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 36 × 600 / (100 + 600) = 30.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 900 Ω and 1800 Ω in parallel (600 Ω) to obtain V = 30.9 V.

items.workedSolution: (a) $I_{\mathrm{tot}} = 0.275 mA$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −11.0 V$. (c) Virtual earth holds the summing junction at zero volts so each input branch current depends only on its own voltage and resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Sums $V_1/R_1 + V_2/R_2 + V_3/R_3$ using virtual earth at node X.

Obtains $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −11.0 V$.
States that node X is held at $0\text{ V}$ (virtual earth) while unsaturated.
Concludes each branch current $V_k/R_k$ is independent of the other inputs.

parts.prompt: Assuming the op-amp initially remains unsaturated with virtual earth at node X, calculate the total current flowing toward node X through the three input resistors (in mA).
Determine the actual output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$, checking for saturation.
Explain why changing one input voltage does not alter the currents in the other input branches while the amplifier stays unsaturated.
parts.expectedAnswer: Virtual earth holds the summing junction at zero volts so each input branch current depends only on its own voltage and resistor.
workingSteps: Because open-loop gain is very large and the amplifier is unsaturated, node X stays at $0\text{ V}$.
Each branch current $V_k/R_k$ is therefore fixed purely by its own input voltage and resistor with zero crosstalk.

items.stem: An ideal 35 V DC source energises an accelerator interlock lamp matrix containing an ideal ammeter A in the main line, a series branch of 8 Ω and 4 Ω resistors, and a parallel 21 Ω resistor, as shown.

markScheme.criterion: Sums 8 Ω and 4 Ω in series before dividing 35 V.
Obtains I_1 = 2.92 A.
Obtains I_2 = 1.67 A.

items.stem: In an electrolysis-cell bypass resistor bank, a uniform platinum-iridium wire R_1 (resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 2 m, area 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) lies in parallel with a 4 Ω shunt, fed via a 10 Ω series resistor from an ideal 28 V DC source. What current passes through the platinum-iridium wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 0.909 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 4)/(R_1 + 4) = 0.741 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 10 + 0.741 = 10.7 Ω; main current I_tot = 2.61 A, V_p = 1.93 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 2.12 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 0.909 Ω and obtains 2.12 A.

items.stem: In the twin-supply test harness shown, both cells have negligible internal resistance, with ε₁ = 13.5 V, R₁ = 4.50 Ω, R₂ = 7.50 Ω, and R₃ = 5.50 Ω. Given that the current in the lower branch is I₃ = 0.850 A, calculate the electromotive force ε₂ of the lower cell.
items.workedSolution: At junction Q, Kirchhoff's first law gives I₂ = I₁ + I₃. Around the upper loop, ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₂R₂ = 0, so I₁ = (ε₁ − I₃R₂) / (R₁ + R₂) = 0.5938 A and I₂ = 1.444 A. Around the lower loop, ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 15.50 V. Hence the required answer is 15.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's first and second laws to obtain 15.5 V.

items.stem: In the schematic for a portable defibrillator battery module, a non-ideal cell (ε = 47.12 V, r = 1.3 Ω) supplies a single 23.5 Ω resistive load. What power is dissipated in the 23.5 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 47.12 / (23.5 + 1.3) = 1.90 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 47.12 − (1.90)(1.3) = 44.6 V. External load power P = I² R = 84.8 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 84.8 W.

items.stem: An inverting op-amp has $R_{\mathrm{in}} = 5.00\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 100\text{ k}\Omega$, and saturation voltage $\pm 12.5\text{ V}$. An input of $+900\text{ mV}$ is connected. What is the actual output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$?
items.workedSolution: Ideal output $= -\frac{100}{5.00} \times 0.900\text{ V} = -18.0\text{ V}$. Because $|-18.0\text{ V}| > 12.5\text{ V}$, the op-amp saturates and clamps strictly at $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −12.5 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Clamped output voltage equals −12.5 V.

items.stem: An autonomous drone uses Hall effect sensors in two subsystems: (i) a non-contact rotor tachometer with $5$ magnets on the hub giving a pulse frequency of $150\text{ Hz}$, and (ii) a magnetic attitude probe ($S = 15.0\text{ mV mT}^{-1}$) tilted at $36.9^\circ$ to a $40.0\text{ mT}$ reference field ($V = S B \cos\theta$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $(150/5) \times 60 = 1.80 × 10³ rev min⁻¹$. (b) $V = 15.0 \times 40.0 \times 0.800 = 480 mV$. (c) Hall sensor measures magnetic field alignment to monitor vehicle or spacecraft attitude, and non-contact operation eliminates mechanical wear.

markScheme.criterion: Divides $150\text{ Hz}$ by $5$ magnets and multiplies by $60$.
Correct rotor speed 1.80 × 10³ rev min⁻¹.
Substitutes $15.0 \times 40.0 \times \cos 36.9^\circ$.
Correct Hall voltage 480 mV.
Explains Hall sensor measures magnetic field alignment to monitor vehicle or spacecraft attitude.
Notes non-contact tachometer advantage (no friction/wear/bounce).

Calculate the output voltage of the attitude probe in mV at $\theta = 36.9^\circ$.
Explain how a Hall sensor monitors attitude relative to an external magnetic field and state one advantage of using it as a tachometer.
parts.expectedAnswer: The Hall sensor measures magnetic field alignment to monitor vehicle or spacecraft attitude because its voltage output tracks the perpendicular field component ($\propto \cos\theta$); in a tachometer it requires zero physical contact, avoiding friction and wear.
workingSteps: State Hall sensor measures magnetic field alignment to monitor vehicle or spacecraft attitude.
State non-contact operation eliminates mechanical wear and works reliably in dirty/oily environments.

Its datasheet gives mark time $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$ and space time $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$. Calculate the pulse repetition frequency (PRF).

markScheme.criterion: Pulse repetition frequency equals 6.08 Hz.

parts.prompt: Calculate the circuit current and hence determine the resistance of R₂.
workingSteps: Opposing cells give net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.800 V.
Series current I = V₁ / R₁ = 3.2 / 3200 = 1.000 × 10⁻³ A.
Potential difference V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.600 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 1.600 × 10³ Ω ≈ 1.60 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: In the handheld hot-knife polymer cutter diagram, a cell (ε = 25.02 V, r = 1.6 Ω) supplies a 7.5 Ω external resistor steadily for 120 s. What total energy is delivered to the 7.5 Ω resistor?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 25.02 / (7.5 + 1.6) = 2.75 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 20.6 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 6.80 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 2.75 A and E_ext = I² R t = 6.80 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Refer to the equivalent loop for a solar-buoy accumulator charging loop: a 11 V battery (1.4 Ω internal resistance) charges an opposing 4 V battery (1.7 Ω internal resistance) via 7 Ω and 16 Ω series resistors. What is the potential difference across the 16 Ω load resistor?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 11 − 4 = 7 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 1.4 + 1.7 + 7 + 16 = 26.1 Ω. Loop current I = 7 / 26.1 = 0.268 A. Load p.d. V = 4.29 V and load power P = 1.15 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 4.29 V.

items.stem: In AQA Required Practical 10, a stiff copper wire carrying a steady current I = 4.0 A passes horizontally perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B = 55 mT between magnadur poles mounted on a tared top-pan balance. The active length of wire inside the field is L = 6.0 cm. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) 13.2 mN. (b) 1.35 g. (c) 0.220 N m⁻¹. (d) at fixed current, the magnetic force on the wire and equal-opposite downward force on the magnet scale directly proportionally with both the active wire length inside the uniform field and the magnetic flux density.

markScheme.criterion: Applies F = BIL in SI units.
Obtains F = 13.2 mN.
Divides F by g = 9.81 m s⁻² and converts kg to g.
Obtains Δm = 1.35 g.

items.stem: In Required Practical 9, a charged electrolytic capacitor discharges through a 100 kΩ resistor. Two points on the straight best-fit line of $\ln(V / \mathrm{V})$ against $t$ are $(15\text{ s}, 2.030)$ and $(75\text{ s}, 0.212)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\tau = 33.0 s$ ($T_{1/2} = 22.9 s$). (b) $C = 330 μF$. (c) $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 27.5 s$. (d) observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

markScheme.criterion: Computes negative gradient of $\ln V$ vs $t$ and equates to $-1/\tau$.
Time constant $\tau = 33.0 s$.
Uses $C = \tau / R$ with $R$ in Ω.
Capacitance $C = 330 μF$.
Combines $R$ and $R_V$ in parallel: $1/R_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1/R + 1/R_V$.
Effective time constant $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 27.5 s$.
Match +/− polarity and voltage rating to prevent electrolytic dielectric breakdown.
Voltmeter $R_V \gg R$ prevents parallel leakage current from shortening apparent $\tau$.

items.stem: Two steady operating points are logged in an alkaline lantern-battery rheostat practical: (0.6 A, 11.4 V) and (3.8 A, 6.6 V). Assuming ohmic internal resistance, what is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (11.4 − 6.6)/(3.8 − 0.6) = 1.50 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 11.4 + (0.6)(1.50) = 12.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 1.50 Ω.

items.stem: An ideal 30 V cell powers a galvanometer damping-tap potential divider where upper resistor 8 Ω feeds the parallel combination of lower divider arm 60 Ω and load 120 Ω. What electrical power is delivered to the 120 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (60 × 120)/(60 + 120) = 40.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 30 × 40.0 / (8 + 40.0) = 25.0 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 120 = 0.208 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 120 = 5.21 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (40.0 Ω) to obtain 5.21 W.

items.stem: The diagram shows a matched-impedance ladder built from resistors whose values are multiples of R between terminals P and Q. The top branch contains 12R, and the lower branch consists of R in series with the parallel pair (3R || 6R) and another R. What is the total resistance between P and Q in terms of R?
items.workedSolution: Inner parallel pair: (3R × 6R) / (3R + 6R) = 2R. Lower branch total: R + 2R + R = 4R. Combining in parallel with 12R gives R_PQ = (12 × 4) / (12 + 4) R = 3R.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces the inner parallel pair, series lower branch, and outer parallel combination to obtain 3R.

items.stem: Within a diaphragm pressure-gauge wire arm, resistive element R_1 (titanium, ρ = 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 1.6 m, area 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) forms a series divider with a 12 Ω resistor across 6 V (ideal).

markScheme.criterion: Applies R = ρL / A with given SI values.
Obtains R_1 = 1.34 Ω.
Adds 12 Ω to R_1 and divides 6 V by R_tot.
Obtains I = 0.450 A.
Multiplies I by R_1.
Obtains V_1 = 0.604 V.

items.stem: Two identical ideal cells, each of emf 1.50 V, are connected in parallel to drive a 5.00 Ω load in a twin-AA torch circuit. What reading is shown on the ideal ammeter A in the main branch?
items.workedSolution: Identical ideal cells in parallel maintain terminal pd V = ε = 1.50 V (not 2ε). Main-branch current I = ε / R = 0.3000 A, and each cell supplies I/2 = 0.1500 A. Thus the answer is 0.300 A.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = ε for parallel identical cells to obtain 0.300 A.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor has a potential difference of $4.50\text{ V}$ across it when carrying $0.150\text{ A}$, as marked on its $I\text{–}V$ characteristic.
items.workedSolution: (a) $R = 4.50 / 0.150 = 30.0\,\Omega$. (b) higher temperature liberates many more free charge carriers outweighing lattice vibrations so resistance decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Apply $R = V/I$ directly from coordinates.
Resistance $= 30.0\,\Omega$.
Higher temperature releases many more free charge carriers (higher carrier density n).
Carrier increase dominates over increased lattice vibrations so resistance falls.

Explain why increasing the thermistor's temperature reduces its resistance even though lattice vibrations increase.
parts.expectedAnswer: In an NTC semiconductor, higher temperature liberates many more free charge carriers outweighing lattice vibrations so resistance decreases.
workingSteps: Carrier density n rises steeply with temperature, outweighing increased lattice collisions.

items.stem: A marine navigation beacon RF selector uses a parallel LC tuned circuit with $L = 350\text{ }\mu\text{H}$, $C = 180\text{ pF}$, and quality factor $Q = 55$. At resonance the peak output voltage across the parallel LC network is $V_{\max} = 6.40 V$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_0 = 634 kHz$. (b) Half-power level $= 0.707 V_{\max} = 4.53 V$. (c) $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q = 11.5 kHz$. (d) Higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ with $\mu\text{H}$ and $\text{pF}$ converted to SI.
Obtains $f_0 = 634 kHz$.
Computes $0.707 V_{\max} = 4.53 V$.
Uses $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$.
Obtains $f_{\mathrm{B}} = 11.5 kHz$.
States higher Q improves selectivity against adjacent stations.
States narrower bandwidth can clip/attenuate outer modulating sidebands.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resonant frequency $f_0$ in kHz.
Calculate the voltage level at which the half-power bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ is measured on the resonance graph.
Calculate the bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ of the tuned circuit in kHz.
Explain the trade-off of replacing the coil with a lower-resistance coil to achieve a significantly higher Q factor in an AM broadcast receiver.
parts.expectedAnswer: A higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.
workingSteps: Higher Q sharpens the peak, improving selectivity against neighbouring stations.
However, $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$ shrinks, risking attenuation of high-frequency audio sidebands.

items.stem: A portable FTIR interferometer DC supply uses a battery of emf 23.25 V and internal resistance 2.5 Ω connected to a 7 Ω resistor in series with parallel 10 Ω and 15 Ω resistors, operating steadily for 15 s.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_ext = 13.0 Ω and adds 2.5 Ω internal resistance.
Obtains I = 1.50 A.
Applies V_term = ε − I r or I R_ext.
Obtains V_term = 19.5 V.
Uses E_ext = V_term I × 15.
Obtains E_ext = 439 J.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a portable sensor power block. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.400 A, V₁ = 7.30 V) and (I₂ = 1.60 A, V₂ = 5.80 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.650 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 9.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 32.0 mV when it carries 2.50 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 3.90 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 1.250 Ω ≈ 1.25 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 7.800 V ≈ 7.80 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01280 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.772 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.77 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0768 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 1.25 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 7.80 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0128 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.77 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0768 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 7.3 + 0.4 × 1.250 Ω = 7.800 V ≈ 7.80 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.03200 V / 2.500 A = 0.01280 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.workedSolution: (a) $V_R = V_{\mathrm{s}} - V_{\mathrm{Z}} = 8.90 V$. (b) $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_R / R_{\mathrm{s}} = 40.5 mA$. (c) $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z}} = 206 mW$.

Obtains $V_R = 8.90 V$.
Applies $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_R / R_{\mathrm{s}}$.
Obtains $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = 40.5 mA$.
Uses $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z}}$.
Obtains $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = 206 mW$.

Calculate the reverse operating current flowing through the Zener diode in mA.
workingSteps: Because comparator input current is negligible, $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{s}} - V_{\mathrm{Z}}}{R_{\mathrm{s}}} = 40.5 mA$.

items.stem: Monitoring a satellite battery-deck thermistor divider driven by an ideal 14 V cell, a technician records 4.00 V on an ideal voltmeter across NTC thermistor R_1 (whose resistance drops when warmed) in series with 1050 Ω. What is R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 1050 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 14 − 4.00 = 10.0 V. Current I = 10.0 / 1050 = 9.52 × 10⁻³ A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 4.00 / 9.52 × 10⁻³ = 420 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 10.0 V to find I = 9.52 × 10⁻³ A and R_1 = 420 Ω.

items.stem: In Required Practical 5, a student measures the resistance $R$ of varying lengths $L$ of a nichrome resistance wire of mean diameter $(0.28 \pm 0.01)$ mm. The straight-line graph of $R$ against $L$ has gradient 17.8 Ω m⁻¹ ($\pm 1.8\%$) and vertical intercept 0.35 Ω.
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m²$. (b) $\rho = 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m$. (c) $\%\Delta\rho = 8.94\%$. (d) keep the current low and open the switch between readings to prevent wire heating while the non zero intercept represents contact and lead resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Converts diameter to metres and applies $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m²$.
Uses $\rho = \mathrm{gradient} \times A$ (ignoring intercept).
Resistivity $\rho = 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m$.
Adds gradient percentage uncertainty to twice diameter percentage uncertainty.
Percentage uncertainty $= 8.94\%$.
Open switch / low current prevents Joule heating that would change wire temperature and $\rho$.
Positive intercept represents contact and connecting-lead resistance.

items.stem: In Required Practical 6, a student investigates an aged 6 V lantern battery connected to a 4.7 Ω protective resistor and rheostat. Two well-spaced points on the straight best-fit graph of terminal potential difference $V$ against current $I$ are $(0.20\text{ A}, 5.82\text{ V})$ and $(0.72\text{ A}, 4.73\text{ V})$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $r = 2.10 Ω$. (b) $\varepsilon = 6.24 V$. (c) $I_{\max} = 0.918 A$. (d) include a protective series resistor and open the switch between readings to avoid heating the cell so internal resistance stays constant.

markScheme.criterion: Uses negative gradient of $V$ against $I$ line.
Internal resistance $r = 2.10 Ω$.
Substitutes point into $\varepsilon = V + Ir$.
Emf $\varepsilon = 6.24 V$.
Uses total resistance $r + R_{\mathrm{prot}}$ in $I = \varepsilon / R_{\mathrm{total}}$.
Maximum safe current $= 0.918 A$.
Protective resistor limits current to prevent short-circuit overheating.
Opening switch between readings prevents cell heating/draining so $r$ and $\varepsilon$ stay constant.

items.stem: An open-loop op-amp voltage comparator with saturation limits $\pm 13.5\text{ V}$ has a fixed reference $V_- = 5.40\text{ V}$ on its inverting input and a sensor potential $V_+ = 5.10\text{ V}$ on its non-inverting input. What is the output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$?
items.workedSolution: With no negative feedback, $V_{\mathrm{out}} = A_{\mathrm{OL}}(V_+ - V_-)$. Since $V_+ - V_- = -0.30\text{ V} < 0$ and $A_{\mathrm{OL}}$ is huge, the output saturates at the negative rail: $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −13.5 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Comparator output voltage equals −13.5 V.

items.stem: Current from an ideal 52.8 V supply enters an avionics redundant bus monitor via a 12 Ω series resistor before dividing across 40 Ω, 60 Ω, and 24 Ω parallel elements. What current flows through the 40 Ω branch?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/40 + 1/60 + 1/24, giving R_p = 12.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 12 + 12.0 = 24.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 52.8 / 24.0 = 2.20 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 26.4 V, and I(40 Ω) = V_p / 40 = 0.660 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 0.660 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 12.3 Ω and combines in parallel with 8 Ω.
Obtains R_p = 4.84 Ω.
Adds 2 Ω to R_p and uses I = V / R_tot.

Finds V_p and uses P_1 = V_p² / R_1.
Obtains P_1 = 52.9 W.

items.stem: The circuit diagram shows a multi-loop diagnostics rig with two ideal cells of negligible internal resistance. Component values are ε₁ = 15.0 V, R₁ = 6.00 Ω, R₂ = 9.00 Ω, and R₃ = 4.50 Ω. The steady current in the bottom branch is measured as I₃ = 0.800 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Based on conservation of electric charge. (b) I₁ = 0.5200 A ≈ 0.520 A, so I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = 1.320 A ≈ 1.32 A. (c) ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 15.48 V ≈ 15.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: States conservation of electric charge.
Substitutes I₂ = I₁ + I₃ into ε₁ = I₁R₁ + I₂R₂ correctly.
Correct current I₁ = 0.520 A (and I₂ = 1.32 A).
Correctly evaluates middle-branch current I₂ = I₁ + I₃ and states ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Substitutes I₂R₂ and I₃R₃ consistently into the lower-loop equation.
Correct electromotive force ε₂ = 15.5 V.

items.stem: In the student polarity test loop shown, two ideal cells of electromotive forces ε₁ = 1.50 V and ε₂ = 4.50 V are connected in opposition in series with R₁ = 1.50 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. An ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 1.80 V. What is the resistance of R₂?
items.workedSolution: Since the positive terminals face each other, net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 3.000 V. Current I = V₁ / R₁ = 1.200 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across R₂ is V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.200 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 1.000 × 10³ Ω ≈ 1.00 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses opposing net emf ε₂ − ε₁ = 3.00 V to find R₂ = 1.00 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: In Required Practical 9, a 220 μF capacitor discharges through a 82 kΩ resistor while monitored by a voltmeter of finite resistance 0.4 MΩ connected in parallel. Calculate the actual measured time constant $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
items.workedSolution: Ideal time constant $\tau = RC = 18.0 s$, $C = 220$ μF, $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2 = 12.5 s$, and with parallel voltmeter $R_{\mathrm{eff}} = R R_V / (R + R_V)$, $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 15.0 s$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines effectiveTauWithMeterS $= 15.0 s$.

items.stem: Testing a meteorological sunshine-duration logger supplied at 24 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 123 kΩ in darkness to 1.5 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 8 kΩ resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 123 + 8 = 131 kΩ, so I_dark = 24 / 131000 = 1.83 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.47 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 24 × 8 / (1.5 + 8) = 20.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 20.2 V.

items.stem: The schematic of a mobile lidar scanner power distribution box shows emf 40.75 V with internal resistance 1.3 Ω driving 9 Ω in series with 9 Ω ∥ 18 Ω for 100 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) R_p = 6.00 Ω, R_tot = 16.3 Ω, I = 2.50 A. (b) P_source = ε I = 102 W. (c) V_term = 37.5 V, so E_ext = V_term I t = 9.38 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_tot including R_p, R_s, and r.
Obtains I = 2.50 A.
Applies P_source = ε I.
Obtains P_source = 102 W.
Finds terminal p.d. 37.5 V and multiplies by I and 100 s.
Obtains E_ext = 9.38 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Within a linear displacement slide-wire sensor, 1.6 m of uniform titanium wire R_1 (area 2.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) shares an ideal 16 V rail in series with a 17 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the titanium wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m)(1.6) / (2.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 3.36 Ω. Series current I = 16 / (17 + 3.36) = 0.786 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 2.64 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 3.36 Ω and obtains 2.64 V.

items.stem: In the robot sensor bus shown, two identical ideal cells of emf 4.80 V are wired in parallel across a 16.0 Ω resistor with an ideal ammeter A and voltmeter V.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = ε = 4.80 V, so I = ε / R = 0.300 A. (b) identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current.

markScheme.criterion: Correct ammeter reading 0.300 A.
States that identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current.

workingSteps: For identical cells in parallel, V = ε = 4.80 V.

parts.prompt: Explain why connecting identical cells in parallel does not double the voltmeter reading.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current, the potential difference across both branches remains equal to the electromotive force of a single cell.
workingSteps: Each charge passes through only one cell on any closed loop, so parallel cells share current rather than adding energy per coulomb.

items.stem: Which statement gives the complete, exam-accurate statement of Ohm's law for a metallic conductor?
items.workedSolution: Ohm's law requires both direct proportionality ($I \propto V$) AND constant temperature / physical conditions. Therefore option C is correct: current is directly proportional to potential difference provided temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: current is directly proportional to potential difference provided temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

options.text: According to Ohm's law, resistance equals potential difference divided by current for every device at all temperatures
options.distractorRationale: R = V/I is the universal definition of resistance, NOT Ohm's law; Ohm's law requires constant temperature / physical conditions.

options.label: B
options.text: According to Ohm's law, current is inversely proportional to potential difference when temperature rises
options.distractorRationale: Current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: According to Ohm's law, current is directly proportional to potential difference provided temperature and physical conditions remain constant

options.label: D
options.text: According to Ohm's law, power is directly proportional to current regardless of heating
options.distractorRationale: P = I²R scales quadratically with current at constant R.

items.stem: An LC tuner resonance curve reaches a peak output voltage $V_{\max} = 10.0\text{ V}$ at $f_0$. At what output voltage level must the bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ be measured on the resonance curve?
items.workedSolution: Because power $P \propto V^2$, half-power occurs at $V = \frac{V_{\max}}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.707 V_{\max} = 0.707 \times 10.0 = 7.07 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Half-power bandwidth level equals 7.07 V.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Confuses RC time-constant factor $1 - e^{-1} = 0.632$ with half-power $1/\sqrt{2}$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Confuses exponential decay $e^{-1} = 0.368$ with half-power amplitude.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a rechargeable NiMH pack. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.400 A, V₁ = 3.36 V) and (I₂ = 1.60 A, V₂ = 2.64 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.450 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 7.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 24.0 mV when it carries 2.00 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 1.80 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 0.6000 Ω ≈ 0.600 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 3.600 V ≈ 3.60 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01200 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.867 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.87 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0480 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 0.600 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 3.60 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0120 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.87 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0480 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 3.36 + 0.4 × 0.6000 Ω = 3.600 V ≈ 3.60 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02400 V / 2.000 A = 0.01200 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: Why is an enhancement MOSFET preferred over a bipolar junction transistor when switching a motor directly from a high-resistance sensor or CMOS logic output?
items.workedSolution: Because the metal gate is isolated by an oxide layer, an insulated silicon dioxide gate gives virtually infinite input resistance drawing negligible gate current, avoiding loading the preceding circuit.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that insulated silicon dioxide gate gives virtually infinite input resistance drawing negligible gate current.

items.stem: In a spectrometer slit-warmer wire element, a uniform cylindrical titanium wire R_1 of resistivity 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 4.3 m, and diameter 0.7 mm is wired directly across an ideal 15 V DC source, as shown. What is the electrical resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.7 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 3.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 4.69 Ω. Current I = 15 / 4.69 = 3.20 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 47.9 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 4.69 Ω.

options.text: Force the R against L line through the origin because resistance must always equal zero at L = 0.

options.text: Keep the current low and open the switch between readings to prevent wire heating while the non zero intercept represents contact and lead resistance.

options.label: D
options.text: Use constantan because its resistivity increases dramatically with small temperature rises.
options.distractorRationale: Constantan is chosen specifically for its very low temperature coefficient of resistivity.

items.stem: During Required Practical 6 using a two-cell laboratory battery pack, the $V$ against $I$ line passes through $(0.15\text{ A}, 2.91\text{ V})$ and $(0.55\text{ A}, 2.35\text{ V})$. Calculate the electromotive force $\varepsilon$ of the battery.
items.workedSolution: From $V = \varepsilon - Ir$, gradient $-r = (2.35 - 2.91)/(0.55 - 0.15) = -1.40$ Ω, $\varepsilon = 3.12$ V, and $I_{\max} = \varepsilon/(r + R_{\mathrm{prot}}) = 0.664 A$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines emfV $= 3.12 V$.

items.stem: On an analogue moving-coil meter bench, resistors of 140 Ω and 160 Ω form a series divider across an ideal 35 V DC supply. A finite-resistance voltmeter (480 Ω, drawn as the parallel branch) is placed across the 160 Ω resistor. What reading does the voltmeter show?
items.workedSolution: The 480 Ω voltmeter shunts the 160 Ω resistor: R_p = (160 × 480)/(160 + 480) = 120 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 35 × 120 / (140 + 120) = 16.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 160 Ω and 480 Ω in parallel (120 Ω) to obtain V = 16.2 V.

items.stem: A balanced thermocouple difference amplifier uses matched resistor pairs $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 240\text{ k}\Omega$ with saturation limits $\pm 13.0 V$. Sensor inputs are $V_- = 2.60 V$ and $V_+ = 3.30 V$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $G_{\mathrm{diff}} = 24.0$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 13.0 V$. (c) Equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $G_{\mathrm{diff}} = R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$.
Obtains 24.0.
Computes $(V_+ - V_-)R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$ and enforces $\pm V_{\mathrm{sat}}$ clipping.
Obtains 13.0 V.
States that equal noise adds identically to both inputs.
Concludes that subtraction eliminates common-mode noise at the output.

Determine the output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$, checking against the saturation rails.
workingSteps: Exceeds $+13.0 V$ rail, so clamps at 13.0 V.

parts.prompt: Explain why 50 Hz mains interference picked up equally on both thermocouple leads does not corrupt $V_{\mathrm{out}}$.
parts.expectedAnswer: Equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.
workingSteps: Adding identical noise $v_{\mathrm{n}}$ to both $V_+$ and $V_-$ leaves $(V_+ + v_{\mathrm{n}}) - (V_- + v_{\mathrm{n}}) = V_+ - V_-$.
Equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.

items.stem: Three parallel resistive loads (14 Ω, 21 Ω, and 42 Ω) in a seismic vault telemetry distribution hub draw power through a 6 Ω line resistor from an ideal 23.4 V cell.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3 and inverts.
Obtains R_p = 7.00 Ω.
Adds 6 Ω to R_p and uses I = V / R_tot.
Obtains I_tot = 1.80 A.
Calculates V_p = 12.6 V and divides by 14 Ω.
Obtains I_1 = 0.900 A.

items.stem: The cryostat parallel heater-and-bypass stage schematic shows an ideal 13 V supply driving a 8 Ω resistor in series with the parallel pair of stainless-steel wire R_1 (L = 6.5 m, A = 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and 11 Ω. What current passes through the stainless-steel wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 8.51 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 11)/(R_1 + 11) = 4.80 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 8 + 4.80 = 12.8 Ω; main current I_tot = 1.02 A, V_p = 4.87 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 0.573 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 8.51 Ω and obtains 0.573 A.

items.stem: The diagram shows a dual-battery bench circuit containing two cells of negligible internal resistance. In the upper branch ε₁ = 12.0 V and R₁ = 4.00 Ω; in the shared middle branch R₂ = 6.00 Ω; and in the bottom branch R₃ = 5.00 Ω carries a current I₃ = 0.800 A. What is the current I₁ in the upper branch?
items.workedSolution: At junction Q, Kirchhoff's first law gives I₂ = I₁ + I₃. Around the upper loop, ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₂R₂ = 0, so I₁ = (ε₁ − I₃R₂) / (R₁ + R₂) = 0.7200 A and I₂ = 1.520 A. Around the lower loop, ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 13.12 V. Hence the required answer is 0.720 A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's first and second laws to obtain 0.720 A.

items.stem: A starter-solenoid test battery of emf 8.93 V and internal resistance 0.7 Ω is wired directly across a 4 Ω external resistor, as shown. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 8.93 / (4 + 0.7) = 1.90 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 8.93 − (1.90)(0.7) = 7.60 V. External load power P = I² R = 14.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 7.60 V.

items.stem: A non-inverting amplifier uses $R_1 = 8.00\text{ k}\Omega$ to 0 V and feedback resistor $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 72.0\text{ k}\Omega$ with saturation limits $\pm 14.0\text{ V}$. Calculate the output voltage when $V_{\mathrm{in}} = +750\text{ mV}$.
items.workedSolution: Non-inverting gain $G = 1 + \frac{R_{\mathrm{f}}}{R_1} = 1 + \frac{72.0}{8.00} = 10.0$. Thus $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 10.0 \times 0.750\text{ V} = 7.50 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Output voltage equals 7.50 V.

items.stem: An N-channel enhancement MOSFET ($V_{\text{th}} = 2.20\text{ V}$) switches a $45.0\text{ }\Omega$ lamp connected to a $12.0\text{ V}$ rail. When driven at $V_{\text{GS}} = 6.20\text{ V}$, the drain current read from its $I_{\text{D}}$–$V_{\text{DS}}$ characteristic is $200\text{ mA}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $V_{\text{DS}} = 12.0 - 9.00 = 3.00 V$. (b) $P = 3.00 \times 200 = 600 mW$. (c) insulated oxide gate over p-substrate gives very high input resistance and conduction above Vth.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates $V_{\text{load}} = 0.200 \times 45.0 = 9.00\text{ V}$.
Correct $V_{\text{DS}} = 3.00 V$.
Correct dissipation 600 mW.
Identifies n-type drain and source regions in a p-type substrate.
Notes insulating silicon-oxide gate layer causes very high input resistance.
Explains insulated oxide gate over p-substrate gives very high input resistance and conduction above Vth.

parts.prompt: Calculate the circuit current and hence determine the resistance of R₂.
workingSteps: Opposing cells give net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 5.500 V.
Series current I = V₁ / R₁ = 3.5 / 5000 = 7.000 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Potential difference V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 2.000 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 2.857 × 10³ Ω ≈ 2.86 × 10³ Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy dissipated in resistor R₁ during the 3 min interval.

items.stem: The schematic models a battery-powered bottle-warmer pad where a 9.52 V battery (0.7 Ω internal resistance) energises a 12 Ω load for 150 s. Determine the energy dissipated in the 12 Ω resistor.
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 9.52 / (12 + 0.7) = 0.750 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 9.00 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 1.01 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 0.750 A and E_ext = I² R t = 1.01 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Testing Kirchhoff's loop rule on a marine dual-bank isolator test rig, a student connects a 19 V cell (1.8 Ω internal resistance) against an opposing 9 V cell (1.1 Ω internal resistance) through 9 Ω and 5 Ω external resistors (equivalent ε, r illustrated). What steady current circulates around the loop?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 19 − 9 = 10 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 1.8 + 1.1 + 9 + 5 = 16.9 Ω. Loop current I = 10 / 16.9 = 0.592 A. Load p.d. V = 2.96 V and load power P = 1.75 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 0.592 A.

items.stem: In AQA Required Practical 9, a student charges an initially uncharged 820 μF capacitor through a 68 kΩ resistor from a 9.0 V supply, logging capacitor potential difference V_C against time t.
items.workedSolution: (a) 55.8 s. (b) 4.98 V. (c) 0.132 mA. (d) during capacitor charging, plotting ln(V0 minus VC) against time gives a straight line of gradient minus 1/(RC) and vertical intercept ln(V0), while the area under the current-time curve equals total charge stored.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains τ = 55.8 s.
Applies V_C = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).
Obtains V_C = 4.98 V.
Uses I₀ = V₀ / R at t = 0 when V_C = 0.
Obtains I₀ = 0.132 mA.
States plotting ln(V₀ − V_C) vs t yields a straight line of gradient −1/(RC).
States area under I–t curve equals total charge Q stored.

items.stem: In Required Practical 9, a charged electrolytic capacitor discharges through a 47 kΩ resistor. Two points on the straight best-fit line of $\ln(V / \mathrm{V})$ against $t$ are $(10\text{ s}, 1.745)$ and $(50\text{ s}, -0.066)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\tau = 22.1 s$ ($T_{1/2} = 15.3 s$). (b) $C = 470 μF$. (c) $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 21.1 s$. (d) observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

markScheme.criterion: Computes negative gradient of $\ln V$ vs $t$ and equates to $-1/\tau$.
Time constant $\tau = 22.1 s$.
Uses $C = \tau / R$ with $R$ in Ω.
Capacitance $C = 470 μF$.
Combines $R$ and $R_V$ in parallel: $1/R_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1/R + 1/R_V$.
Effective time constant $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 21.1 s$.
Match +/− polarity and voltage rating to prevent electrolytic dielectric breakdown.
Voltmeter $R_V \gg R$ prevents parallel leakage current from shortening apparent $\tau$.

items.stem: Switching between two load settings in a lead-acid standby cell load step test (series loop shown) changes the current from 1.6 A to 6 A while terminal voltage falls from 23.3 V to 9 V. What is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (23.3 − 9)/(6 − 1.6) = 3.25 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 23.3 + (1.6)(3.25) = 28.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 28.5 V.

items.stem: Connecting a 24 Ω resistive load across the 12 Ω lower section of a 15 Ω–12 Ω divider in a bench power-supply reference trim divider supplied at 10 V (ideal) pulls down the output p.d. What loaded output potential difference appears across the 24 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (12 × 24)/(12 + 24) = 8.00 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 10 × 8.00 / (15 + 8.00) = 3.48 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 24 = 0.145 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 24 = 0.504 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (8.00 Ω) to obtain 3.48 V.

items.stem: The diagram shows a precision attenuator board built from resistors whose values are multiples of R between terminals P and Q. The top branch contains 4R, and the lower branch consists of R in series with the parallel pair (3R || 6R) and another R. What is the total resistance between P and Q in terms of R?
items.workedSolution: Inner parallel pair: (3R × 6R) / (3R + 6R) = 2R. Lower branch total: R + 2R + R = 4R. Combining in parallel with 4R gives R_PQ = (4 × 4) / (4 + 4) R = 2R.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces the inner parallel pair, series lower branch, and outer parallel combination to obtain 2R.

items.stem: Across an ideal 20 V source in a cantilever beam strain-wire circuit, a 16 Ω reference resistor precedes cupronickel wire R_1 having length 5.6 m, area 4.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², and resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

Obtains V_1 = 4.99 V.

items.stem: Two identical ideal cells, each of emf 9.00 V, are connected in parallel across a 18.0 Ω resistor in a field-logger power supply, as shown. What is the steady current supplied by each individual cell?
items.workedSolution: Identical ideal cells in parallel maintain terminal pd V = ε = 9.00 V (not 2ε). Main-branch current I = ε / R = 0.5000 A, and each cell supplies I/2 = 0.2500 A. Thus the answer is 0.250 A.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = ε for parallel identical cells to obtain 0.250 A.

items.stem: A student records the current–voltage ($I\text{–}V$) characteristics of a tungsten filament lamp, an NTC thermistor, and a silicon semiconductor diode using the test circuit shown.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Resistance is V divided by I filament ions vibrate more with temperature while thermistor carrier density rises sharply; covers voltmeter parallel / ammeter series / potential divider, strict $R = V/I$ (reject $1/\text{gradient}$), filament lattice vibration collisions, NTC carrier-density surge, and diode forward/reverse threshold.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): States Ohm's law (I ∝ V at constant temperature/physical conditions) and correct test circuit (voltmeter in parallel, ammeter in series, potential divider from 0 V).
L1 (Area 1): Explicitly states resistance at any point is R = V/I — NEVER 1/gradient (citing gradient caps Area 1/2).
L2 (Area 2): Filament lamp: higher current increases filament temperature so positive lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude (reject ions 'moving around').
L2 (Area 2): More frequent collisions between conduction electrons and vibrating lattice ions impede drift, increasing resistance R.
L3 (Area 3): NTC thermistor: higher temperature releases many more free charge carriers (n increases sharply), dominating over lattice vibrations so resistance R decreases.
L3 (Area 3): Semiconductor diode: conducts sharply above forward threshold p.d. (~0.6–0.7 V) with falling (non-zero) resistance, and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

parts.prompt: Describe how to obtain the $I\text{–}V$ characteristic and determine resistance from the graph, and explain microscopically why the resistance of a filament lamp increases with current whereas the resistance of an NTC thermistor decreases, contrasting both with a semiconductor diode.
parts.expectedAnswer: Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the component and the ammeter in series, using a potential divider to sweep potential difference smoothly from $0\text{ V}$ (reversing supply polarity for negative values). Ohm's law ($I \propto V$) holds only at constant temperature; resistance is V divided by I filament ions vibrate more with temperature while thermistor carrier density rises sharply. At any operating point, resistance is strictly $R = V/I$ (never $1/\text{gradient}$). In a filament lamp, larger current heats the tungsten so positive lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude, causing more frequent collisions with conduction electrons and increasing resistance (flattening the $I\text{–}V$ curve). In an NTC thermistor, heating liberates many more free charge carriers ($n$ increases sharply), outweighing increased lattice collisions so resistance drops (curving steeper). A silicon diode conducts sharply in forward bias above a threshold p.d. ($\approx 0.6\text{–}0.7\text{ V}$) with decreasing (non-zero) resistance, and shows extremely high resistance in reverse bias.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): State Ohm's law (I ∝ V at constant T), voltmeter parallel / ammeter series / potential divider, and R = V/I (never 1/gradient).
Area 2 (L2): Filament microscopic explanation: higher T -> larger lattice ion vibration amplitude -> more frequent electron collisions -> higher R.
Area 3 (L3): NTC thermistor (sharp rise in free charge carrier density n outweighs lattice vibrations -> lower R) and diode (threshold ~0.6–0.7 V forward, very high reverse R).

items.stem: A portable AM broadcast front-end amplifier uses a parallel LC tuned circuit with $L = 120\text{ }\mu\text{H}$, $C = 300\text{ pF}$, and quality factor $Q = 80$. At resonance the peak output voltage across the parallel LC network is $V_{\max} = 9.20 V$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_0 = 839 kHz$. (b) Half-power level $= 0.707 V_{\max} = 6.51 V$. (c) $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q = 10.5 kHz$. (d) Higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ with $\mu\text{H}$ and $\text{pF}$ converted to SI.
Obtains $f_0 = 839 kHz$.
Computes $0.707 V_{\max} = 6.51 V$.
Uses $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$.
Obtains $f_{\mathrm{B}} = 10.5 kHz$.
States higher Q improves selectivity against adjacent stations.
States narrower bandwidth can clip/attenuate outer modulating sidebands.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resonant frequency $f_0$ in kHz.
Calculate the voltage level at which the half-power bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ is measured on the resonance graph.
Calculate the bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ of the tuned circuit in kHz.
Explain the trade-off of replacing the coil with a lower-resistance coil to achieve a significantly higher Q factor in an AM broadcast receiver.
parts.expectedAnswer: A higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.
workingSteps: Higher Q sharpens the peak, improving selectivity against neighbouring stations.
However, $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$ shrinks, risking attenuation of high-frequency audio sidebands.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a student investigation battery. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.350 A, V₁ = 3.96 V) and (I₂ = 1.55 A, V₂ = 3.12 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.500 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 8.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 23.0 mV when it carries 2.20 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 2.00 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 0.7000 Ω ≈ 0.700 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 4.200 V ≈ 4.20 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01045 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.673 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0418 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 0.700 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 4.20 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0105 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.67 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0418 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 3.955 + 0.35 × 0.7000 Ω = 4.200 V ≈ 4.20 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02300 V / 2.200 A = 0.01045 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: During a laboratory $I$–$V$ investigation, a 9.10 V Zener diode is reverse-biased in series with a 330 Ω protective resistor across an 18.0 V bench supply, with no external current drawn from the reference terminal.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = 27.0 mA$. (b) $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = 245 mW$. (c) It conducts near 0.7 V in forward bias like a silicon diode while reverse bias blocks current until sharp avalanche breakdown at the Zener voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$ from $V_{\mathrm{s}}$ and divides by $R_{\mathrm{s}}$.
Obtains $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = 27.0 mA$.
Applies $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z}}$.
Obtains $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = 245 mW$.
States forward bias conducts near $0.7\text{ V}$ like an ordinary silicon diode.
States reverse bias blocks current until sharp nearly vertical breakdown at $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the reverse breakdown current through the Zener diode in mA.
Calculate the thermal power dissipated by the Zener diode in mW.
Compare the forward-bias and reverse-bias regions of the Zener diode $I$–$V$ characteristic shown in the diagram.
parts.expectedAnswer: A Zener diode conducts near 0.7 V in forward bias like a silicon diode while reverse bias blocks current until sharp avalanche breakdown at the Zener voltage.
workingSteps: In forward bias, current rises rapidly near $+0.7\text{ V}$ just like a standard silicon diode.
In reverse bias, current remains negligible until reverse potential reaches $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$, where controlled avalanche breakdown produces a nearly vertical rise in reverse current.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 540 Ω resistor across an ideal 27 V source in a water-bath thermostat calibration circuit, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 18.0 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 540 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 27 − 18.0 = 9.00 V. Current I = 9.00 / 540 = 0.0167 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 18.0 / 0.0167 = 1.08 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 9.00 V to find I = 0.0167 A and R_1 = 1.08 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: In Required Practical 5, a student measures the resistance $R$ of varying lengths $L$ of a constantan wire of mean diameter $(0.32 \pm 0.01)$ mm. The straight-line graph of $R$ against $L$ has gradient 6.1 Ω m⁻¹ ($\pm 2.0\%$) and vertical intercept 0.24 Ω.
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m²$. (b) $\rho = 4.91 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m$. (c) $\%\Delta\rho = 8.25\%$. (d) keep the current low and open the switch between readings to prevent wire heating while the non zero intercept represents contact and lead resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Converts diameter to metres and applies $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m²$.
Uses $\rho = \mathrm{gradient} \times A$ (ignoring intercept).
Resistivity $\rho = 4.91 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m$.
Adds gradient percentage uncertainty to twice diameter percentage uncertainty.
Percentage uncertainty $= 8.25\%$.
Open switch / low current prevents Joule heating that would change wire temperature and $\rho$.
Positive intercept represents contact and connecting-lead resistance.
