items.stem: In Required Practical 6, a student investigates a zinc-carbon dry cell connected to a 2.2 Ω protective resistor and rheostat. Two well-spaced points on the straight best-fit graph of terminal potential difference $V$ against current $I$ are $(0.12\text{ A}, 1.46\text{ V})$ and $(0.44\text{ A}, 1.19\text{ V})$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $r = 0.850 Ω$. (b) $\varepsilon = 1.56 V$. (c) $I_{\max} = 0.511 A$. (d) include a protective series resistor and open the switch between readings to avoid heating the cell so internal resistance stays constant.

markScheme.criterion: Uses negative gradient of $V$ against $I$ line.
Internal resistance $r = 0.850 Ω$.
Substitutes point into $\varepsilon = V + Ir$.
Emf $\varepsilon = 1.56 V$.
Uses total resistance $r + R_{\mathrm{prot}}$ in $I = \varepsilon / R_{\mathrm{total}}$.
Maximum safe current $= 0.511 A$.
Protective resistor limits current to prevent short-circuit overheating.
Opening switch between readings prevents cell heating/draining so $r$ and $\varepsilon$ stay constant.

items.stem: A two-input summing amplifier ($R_{\mathrm{f}} = 80\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_2 = 20\text{ k}\Omega$) operates from $\pm 13.0\text{ V}$ saturation rails. If $V_1 = +1.50\text{ V}$ and $V_2 = +1.00\text{ V}$, what is the actual output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$?
items.workedSolution: Unsaturated formula gives $-80(1.50/10 + 1.00/20) = -16.0\text{ V}$. Because this exceeds the $-13.0\text{ V}$ rail, the output saturates at $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −13.0 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Clamped output voltage equals −13.0 V.

items.stem: Two parallel branches inside a titration pump manifold—one comprising 14 Ω and 7 Ω in series, the other a single 9 Ω resistor—draw current from an ideal 28 V rail through ideal ammeter A. What does A read?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 14 + 7 = 21 Ω, so I_1 = 28 / 21 = 1.33 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 28 / 9 = 3.11 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 4.44 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 1.33 A and 3.11 A to obtain 4.44 A.

items.stem: The circuit diagram shows an engineering teaching circuit with two ideal cells of negligible internal resistance. Component values are ε₁ = 12.5 V, R₁ = 5.00 Ω, R₂ = 5.00 Ω, and R₃ = 6.00 Ω. The steady current in the bottom branch is measured as I₃ = 1.10 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Based on conservation of electric charge. (b) I₁ = 0.7000 A ≈ 0.700 A, so I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = 1.800 A ≈ 1.80 A. (c) ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 15.60 V ≈ 15.6 V.

markScheme.criterion: States conservation of electric charge.

parts.prompt: State the fundamental conservation law on which Kirchhoff's first law is based.
parts.expectedAnswer: Kirchhoff's first law is based on the conservation of electric charge.
workingSteps: Current entering a junction equals current leaving because charge cannot accumulate.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's laws to the upper loop and junction Q to calculate the current I₁ in the upper branch (and hence find I₂).
workingSteps: At junction Q: I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = I₁ + 1.10 A.
Middle branch: I₂ = 0.7000 A + 1.100 A = 1.800 A ≈ 1.80 A.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's second law to the lower loop to determine the electromotive force ε₂.
workingSteps: State lower-loop equation: ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Calculate potential drop across R₂: I₂R₂ = 1.800 A × 5 = 9.000 V.
Add potential drop across R₃: ε₂ = 9.000 V + 6.600 V = 15.60 V ≈ 15.6 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ε / (R + r).
Obtains I = 1.00 A.
Uses V = ε − I r or V = I R_load.
Obtains V = 11.5 V.
Uses P = V I or I² R_load with external quantities.
Obtains P = 11.5 W.

items.stem: The diagram shows an inverting op-amp stage built with $R_{\mathrm{in}} = 10.0 kΩ$ and $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 160 kΩ$. The op-amp has saturation rails $\pm 13.0 V$ and a gain–bandwidth product of 1.60 MHz. An input signal of $+500 mV$ is applied.
items.workedSolution: (a) $G = −16.0$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −8.00 V$. (c) Max unsaturated input $= 813 mV$. (d) Bandwidth $= \mathrm{GBP}/|G| = 100 kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $G = -R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_{\mathrm{in}}$.
Obtains $G = −16.0$.
Computes $G V_{\mathrm{in}}$ and checks against $\pm V_{\mathrm{sat}}$.
Obtains $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −8.00 V$.
Applies $V_{\mathrm{in,max}} = V_{\mathrm{sat}}/|G|$.
Obtains 813 mV.
Applies $\mathrm{BW} = \mathrm{GBP}/|G|$.
Obtains 100 kHz.

items.stem: An attitude-monitoring Hall sensor with sensitivity $12.0\text{ mV mT}^{-1}$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field of $50.0\text{ mT}$. When the craft tilts so the sensor normal lies at $60.0^\circ$ to the field ($V = S B \cos\theta$), what output voltage does the Hall probe produce?
items.workedSolution: $V = 12.0\text{ mV mT}^{-1} \times 50.0\text{ mT} \times \cos 60.0^\circ = 600 \times 0.500 = 300 mV$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 300 mV.

items.stem: A laboratory strobe timing oscillator uses an RC astable timing circuit producing the waveforms shown, with $R_1 = 40.0 kΩ$, $R_2 = 20.0 kΩ$, and $C = 5.00 μF$. Its datasheet specifies $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$ and $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 210 ms$. (b) $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 70.0 ms$. (c) $\mathrm{PRF} = 1/(t_{\mathrm{H}} + t_{\mathrm{L}}) = 3.57 Hz$. (d) Mark-to-space ratio $= 3.00$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$.
Obtains 210 ms.
Uses $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$.
Obtains 70.0 ms.
Sums $T = t_{\mathrm{H}} + t_{\mathrm{L}}$ in seconds and takes $1/T$.
Obtains 3.57 Hz.
Mark-to-space ratio $= 3.00$.

items.stem: In the dual-cell resistor circuit shown, two ideal cells of electromotive forces ε₁ = 3.00 V and ε₂ = 7.50 V are connected in opposition in series with R₁ = 3.00 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. An ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 2.70 V. What is the resistance of R₂?
items.workedSolution: Since the positive terminals face each other, net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.500 V. Current I = V₁ / R₁ = 9.000 × 10⁻⁴ A. Potential difference across R₂ is V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.800 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 2.000 × 10³ Ω ≈ 2.00 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses opposing net emf ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.50 V to find R₂ = 2.00 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: In AQA Required Practical 9, a student records capacitor potential difference V_C against time t while charging an initially uncharged capacitor through a resistor R from a steady supply V₀. How are the charging curve and its linear log plot interpreted?
items.workedSolution: Rearranging V_C = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)) gives V₀ − V_C = V₀ e^(−t/RC), so ln(V₀ − V_C) = ln(V₀) − t/(RC). Therefore the correct statement is: From V_C = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)), during capacitor charging, plotting ln(V0 minus VC) against time gives a straight line of gradient minus 1/(RC) and vertical intercept ln(V0), while the area under the current-time curve equals total charge stored.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: during capacitor charging, plotting ln(V0 minus VC) against time gives a straight line of gradient minus 1/(RC) and vertical intercept ln(V0), while the area under the current-time curve equals total charge stored.

options.text: Plotting ln(V_C) directly against time t produces a straight line of gradient −1/(RC) during charging.
options.distractorRationale: ln(V_C) is linear only during *discharging*; during charging, V₀ − V_C = V₀ e^(−t/RC), so ln(V₀ − V_C) vs t is linear.

options.label: B
options.text: From V_C = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)), during capacitor charging, plotting ln(V0 minus VC) against time gives a straight line of gradient minus 1/(RC) and vertical intercept ln(V0), while the area under the current-time curve equals total charge stored.

options.label: C
options.text: The area under the capacitor voltage–time curve equals the total charge stored on the plates.
options.distractorRationale: Total charge Q equals the area under the *current–time* (I–t) curve, and gradient of Q–t equals I.

options.label: D
options.text: The gradient of the V_C–t charging graph stays constant until V_C reaches V₀ and then abruptly drops to zero.
options.distractorRationale: As V_C rises, V_R = V₀ − V_C and charging current I = V_R/R decay exponentially, making the V_C–t curve progressively shallower.

items.workedSolution: RP9 mark-scheme precision: Confirm constant halving time T₁/₂ across successive equal-ratio drops; in the circuit, observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

markScheme.criterion: Confirm constant halving time T₁/₂ across successive equal-ratio drops; in the circuit, observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm that V drops by an equal number of volts every 10 seconds.
options.distractorRationale: Equal absolute voltage drops describe linear decay, whereas exponential decay has equal fractional drops in equal time intervals.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm that the area under the V against t graph equals the charge stored.
options.distractorRationale: Area under I vs t equals charge Q; area under V vs t equals Q R.

options.label: C
options.text: Confirm constant halving time T₁/₂ across successive equal-ratio drops; in the circuit, observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

options.label: D
options.text: Connect a second resistor in parallel with the voltmeter to raise the measured time constant.
options.distractorRationale: Adding any parallel resistor lowers effective resistance and shortens the time constant further.

items.stem: In the observatory dome-shutter safety sensor diagram, an LDR (137 kΩ dark; 0.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 6 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 6 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 137 + 6 = 143 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 143000 = 8.39 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.503 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 6 / (0.5 + 6) = 11.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 6 kΩ resistor to obtain 8.39 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: A busbar voltage-drop monitor places a 14 Ω reference resistor in series with a uniform nichrome wire R_1 (resistivity 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, length 4 m, area 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) across an ideal 22 V DC source, as shown. What current flows through the series circuit?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m)(4) / (5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 8.00 Ω. Series current I = 22 / (14 + 8.00) = 1.00 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 8.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 8.00 Ω and obtains 1.00 A.

items.stem: An ideal 48 V power unit energises an industrial kiln damper actuator network made from a 14 Ω series element followed by 24 Ω and 48 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (24 × 48)/(24 + 48) = 16.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 14 + 16.0 = 30.0 Ω. Supply current I = 48 / 30.0 = 1.60 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 14 Ω with R_p = 16.0 Ω to obtain I = 1.60 A.

items.stem: In the solar storage test rig shown, two identical ideal cells of emf 12.0 V are wired in parallel across a 30.0 Ω resistor with an ideal ammeter A and voltmeter V.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = ε = 12.0 V, so I = ε / R = 0.400 A. (b) identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current.

markScheme.criterion: Correct ammeter reading 0.400 A.
States that identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current.

parts.prompt: Calculate the reading on the ammeter A.
workingSteps: For identical cells in parallel, V = ε = 12.0 V.

parts.prompt: Explain why connecting identical cells in parallel does not double the voltmeter reading.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current, the potential difference across both branches remains equal to the electromotive force of a single cell.
workingSteps: Each charge passes through only one cell on any closed loop, so parallel cells share current rather than adding energy per coulomb.

items.stem: A forward-biased silicon diode conducts a current of $35.0\text{ mA}$ ($0.0350\text{ A}$) when the potential difference across it is $0.840\text{ V}$. At this point the tangent slope is $0.167\text{ A V}^{-1}$. Calculate the diode's resistance at this operating point.

markScheme.criterion: Diode resistance $R = V/I = 24.0 Ω$ (24.0 Ω, option B).

items.stem: A high-Q radio RF stage ($L = 150\text{ }\mu\text{H}$, $C = 150\text{ pF}$, $Q = 75.0$) has a symmetric resonance peak centred on $f_0$. Calculate the upper $-3\text{ dB}$ cut-off frequency $f_2$ in kHz.
items.workedSolution: $f_0 = 1.06 × 10³ kHz$ and $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q = 14.1 kHz$. Hence $f_2 = f_0 + \frac{f_{\mathrm{B}}}{2} = 1.07 × 10³ kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Upper cut-off frequency equals 1.07 × 10³ kHz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ rather than upper cut-off frequency $f_0 + f_{\mathrm{B}}/2$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an erroneous factor of one-half during rearrangement.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the target quantity by omitting a factor of two.

items.stem: In the forestry fire-tower radio and beacon bus diagram, a non-ideal source (ε = 57 V, r = 1 Ω) feeds a 8 Ω line resistor ahead of parallel 15 Ω and 30 Ω loads. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 50 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (15 × 30)/(15 + 30) = 10.0 Ω, R_ext = 8 + 10.0 = 18.0 Ω, and R_tot = 18.0 + 1 = 19.0 Ω. Current I = 57 / 19.0 = 3.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 57 − (3.00)(1) = 54.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 8.10 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 8.10 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of an alkaline D-cell pack. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.400 A, V₁ = 5.68 V) and (I₂ = 1.40 A, V₂ = 4.88 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.500 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 8.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 22.0 mV when it carries 2.00 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 2.50 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 0.8000 Ω ≈ 0.800 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01100 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.760 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.76 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0550 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 0.800 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 6.00 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0110 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.76 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0550 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 5.68 + 0.4 × 0.8000 Ω = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02200 V / 2.000 A = 0.01100 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: In the MOSFET driver diagram controlling an inductive relay coil, why is a reverse-biased protection diode D connected in parallel across the coil?
items.workedSolution: When the MOSFET abruptly switches OFF, rapid collapse of magnetic flux induces a large back-emf across the coil; a reverse-biased diode across an inductive load provides a safe path for induced current preventing a damaging voltage spike.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that reverse-biased diode across an inductive load provides a safe path for induced current preventing a damaging voltage spike.

items.stem: Refer to the diagram of a precision current-shunt calibration loop: R_1 is a uniform cupronickel wire of circular cross-section (diameter 0.64 mm, length 2.2 m, resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) across 3 V (ideal). What thermal power is dissipated in R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.64 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 3.22 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 2.60 Ω. Current I = 3 / 2.60 = 1.15 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 3.46 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 3.46 W.

items.stem: During Required Practical 5, a nichrome resistance wire of mean diameter 0.28 mm is taped to a metre ruler. Plotting resistance $R$ against length $L$ produces a straight line of gradient 17.8 Ω m⁻¹ with a small positive vertical intercept 0.35 Ω. Calculate the resistivity $\rho$ of the alloy.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area $A = \pi (0.28 \times 10^{-3})^2 / 4 = 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m²$. Resistivity $\rho = \mathrm{gradient} \times A = 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta\rho = 1.8 + 2(3.57) = 8.94\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines resistivityRho $= 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m$.

items.stem: An aged 6 V lantern battery of emf $\varepsilon = 6.24$ V and internal resistance $r = 2.10$ Ω is connected in series with a fixed protective resistor of 4.7 Ω and a variable rheostat (RP6). What is the maximum safe current when the rheostat is reduced to zero?
items.workedSolution: From $V = \varepsilon - Ir$, gradient $-r = (4.73 - 5.82)/(0.72 - 0.2) = -2.10$ Ω, $\varepsilon = 6.24$ V, and $I_{\max} = \varepsilon/(r + R_{\mathrm{prot}}) = 0.918 A$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines maxSafeCurrentA $= 0.918 A$.

items.stem: In a physics teaching potentiometer station, a non-ideal moving-coil ammeter of coil resistance 3.6 Ω (modelled as the 3.6 Ω series element) sits in the main line of an ideal 8 V source feeding parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. What current does the ammeter register?
items.workedSolution: Parallel load R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Including the non-ideal ammeter resistance 3.6 Ω gives R_tot = 3.6 + 3.00 = 6.60 Ω, so I = 8 / 6.60 = 1.21 A.

markScheme.criterion: Includes ammeter coil resistance 3.6 Ω in series with R_p = 3.00 Ω to obtain 1.21 A.

items.stem: A balanced thermocouple difference amplifier uses matched resistor pairs $R_1 = 12\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 180\text{ k}\Omega$ with saturation limits $\pm 12.0 V$. Sensor inputs are $V_- = 1.85 V$ and $V_+ = 2.25 V$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $G_{\mathrm{diff}} = 15.0$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 6.00 V$. (c) Equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $G_{\mathrm{diff}} = R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$.
Obtains 15.0.
Computes $(V_+ - V_-)R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$ and enforces $\pm V_{\mathrm{sat}}$ clipping.
Obtains 6.00 V.
States that equal noise adds identically to both inputs.
Concludes that subtraction eliminates common-mode noise at the output.

parts.prompt: Calculate the differential voltage gain of the circuit.
Determine the output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$, checking against the saturation rails.
Explain why 50 Hz mains interference picked up equally on both thermocouple leads does not corrupt $V_{\mathrm{out}}$.
parts.expectedAnswer: Equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.
workingSteps: Adding identical noise $v_{\mathrm{n}}$ to both $V_+$ and $V_-$ leaves $(V_+ + v_{\mathrm{n}}) - (V_- + v_{\mathrm{n}}) = V_+ - V_-$.
Equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.

items.stem: In a vacuum-evaporator shunted filament holder, a uniform manganin wire R_1 (resistivity 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 2.5 m, area 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) lies in parallel with a 5 Ω shunt, fed via a 2 Ω series resistor from an ideal 29 V DC source. What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 5 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 1.85 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 5)/(R_1 + 5) = 1.35 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 2 + 1.35 = 3.35 Ω; main current I_tot = 8.66 A, V_p = 11.7 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 6.33 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 1.85 Ω and obtains 1.35 Ω.

items.stem: The diagram shows a backup DC power rail containing two cells of negligible internal resistance. In the upper branch ε₁ = 15.0 V and R₁ = 5.00 Ω; in the shared middle branch R₂ = 8.00 Ω; and in the bottom branch R₃ = 4.00 Ω carries a current I₃ = 1.00 A. What is the current I₁ in the upper branch?
items.workedSolution: At junction Q, Kirchhoff's first law gives I₂ = I₁ + I₃. Around the upper loop, ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₂R₂ = 0, so I₁ = (ε₁ − I₃R₂) / (R₁ + R₂) = 0.5385 A and I₂ = 1.538 A. Around the lower loop, ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 16.31 V. Hence the required answer is 0.538 A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's first and second laws to obtain 0.538 A.

items.stem: Load-testing a field transceiver LiFePO4 pack rated at emf 30.02 V with 2.8 Ω internal resistance, a technician connects a 13 Ω resistor across its terminals. What current is delivered by the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 30.02 / (13 + 2.8) = 1.90 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 30.02 − (1.90)(2.8) = 24.7 V. External load power P = I² R = 46.9 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 1.90 A.

items.stem: An inverting ECG amplifier uses $R_{\mathrm{in}} = 10.0\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 250\text{ k}\Omega$, and clips at $\pm 13.5\text{ V}$. What is the maximum input signal amplitude in mV that can be amplified without clipping?
items.workedSolution: Gain magnitude $|G| = \frac{250}{10.0} = 25.0$. Maximum unsaturated input $|V_{\mathrm{in,max}}| = \frac{V_{\mathrm{sat}}}{|G|} = \frac{13.5}{25.0} = 0.540\text{ V} = 540 mV$.

markScheme.criterion: Maximum unsaturated input amplitude equals 540 mV.

items.stem: A silicon photodiode operated in reverse-biased photoconductive mode receives $2.50\text{ mW}$ of optical radiation at a wavelength where its spectral response curve gives a responsivity of $0.520\text{ A W}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 0.520 \times 2.50 \times 10^{-3} = 1.30 × 10³ µA$. (b) Curves are flat vs reverse voltage and evenly spaced vs optical power. (c) reverse-biased photodiode current is proportional to light intensity and pairs with a scintillator for particle detection.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies $0.520 \times 2.50 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$.
Correct photocurrent 1.30 × 10³ µA.
Notes reverse current is nearly independent of reverse bias voltage.
Notes reverse current is directly proportional to light intensity.
Explains reverse-biased photodiode current is proportional to light intensity and pairs with a scintillator for particle detection.
Links flash intensity to a countable electrical pulse.

parts.prompt: Calculate the reverse photocurrent produced in $\mu\text{A}$.
Describe what the reverse-bias $I$–$V$ characteristic curves show about the dependence of photocurrent on (i) reverse voltage and (ii) light intensity.
parts.expectedAnswer: In reverse bias the curves are almost flat (photocurrent is nearly independent of reverse bias voltage), and evenly spaced vertically showing that reverse photocurrent is directly proportional to incident light intensity.
workingSteps: Flat horizontal region → current nearly independent of reverse voltage.
Equal spacing for equal power steps → linear response to light intensity.

parts.prompt: Explain how a photodiode can be combined with a scintillator crystal to detect energetic atomic particles.
parts.expectedAnswer: The reverse-biased photodiode current is proportional to light intensity and pairs with a scintillator for particle detection: each atomic particle excites the scintillator to emit a flash of visible photons, generating a proportional electrical current pulse in the photodiode.
workingSteps: State reverse-biased photodiode current is proportional to light intensity and pairs with a scintillator for particle detection.
Link scintillator light flash to a countable electrical pulse proportional to particle energy.

items.stem: A Schmitt-trigger NOT-gate RC oscillator runs from a 12.0 V supply with an upper switching threshold at $\frac{2}{3} V_{\mathrm{s}}$ and a lower switching threshold at $\frac{1}{3} V_{\mathrm{s}}$. Calculate the width of the hysteresis voltage band between the two thresholds.
items.workedSolution: $V_{\mathrm{UST}} = 8.00\text{ V}$ and $V_{\mathrm{LST}} = 4.00\text{ V}$, giving a hysteresis band of $8.00 - 4.00 = 4.00 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Hysteresis voltage band equals 4.00 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the circuit current and hence determine the resistance of R₂.
workingSteps: Opposing cells give net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.500 V.
Series current I = V₁ / R₁ = 2.7 / 3600 = 7.500 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Potential difference V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.800 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 2.400 × 10³ Ω ≈ 2.40 × 10³ Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy dissipated in resistor R₁ during the 2 min interval.

items.stem: During a 150 s activation of a wax-melting stylus heater loop, a source of emf 30.8 V and internal resistance 1.9 Ω drives a 13.5 Ω load. Calculate the electrical energy transferred to the external load.
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 30.8 / (13.5 + 1.9) = 2.00 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 27.0 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 8.10 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 2.00 A and E_ext = I² R t = 8.10 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Testing Kirchhoff's loop rule on an emergency backup DC bus tie circuit, a student connects a 9 V cell (1.8 Ω internal resistance) against an opposing 4 V cell (1.3 Ω internal resistance) through 7 Ω and 11 Ω external resistors (equivalent ε, r illustrated). What thermal power is dissipated in the 11 Ω load resistor?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 9 − 4 = 5 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 1.8 + 1.3 + 7 + 11 = 21.1 Ω. Loop current I = 5 / 21.1 = 0.237 A. Load p.d. V = 2.61 V and load power P = 0.618 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 0.618 W.

items.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes repeatability from reproducibility in AQA A-Level Physics practical work (Section 3.1.2)?
items.workedSolution: Same person + same apparatus + same method = repeatable; different person/apparatus/method achieving consistent results = reproducible. Therefore the correct statement is: According to standard experimental terminology, repeatability means the original experimenter gets consistent results using the same apparatus and method, whereas reproducibility means different experimenters or apparatus obtain consistent results.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: repeatability means the original experimenter gets consistent results using the same apparatus and method, whereas reproducibility means different experimenters or apparatus obtain consistent results.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeatability proves that systematic zero errors are absent, whereas reproducibility measures instrument resolution.
options.distractorRationale: Consistent repeated readings can still share a hidden systematic offset; reproducibility helps expose systematic bias.

options.text: Repeatability and reproducibility both mean that a measurement agrees closely with the published textbook true value.
options.distractorRationale: Agreement with the true value defines accuracy, not repeatability or reproducibility.

items.stem: In Required Practical 9, a charged electrolytic capacitor discharges through a 82 kΩ resistor. Two points on the straight best-fit line of $\ln(V / \mathrm{V})$ against $t$ are $(8\text{ s}, 1.859)$ and $(44\text{ s}, -0.136)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\tau = 18.0 s$ ($T_{1/2} = 12.5 s$). (b) $C = 220 μF$. (c) $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 15.0 s$. (d) observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

markScheme.criterion: Computes negative gradient of $\ln V$ vs $t$ and equates to $-1/\tau$.
Time constant $\tau = 18.0 s$.
Uses $C = \tau / R$ with $R$ in Ω.
Capacitance $C = 220 μF$.
Combines $R$ and $R_V$ in parallel: $1/R_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1/R + 1/R_V$.
Effective time constant $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 15.0 s$.
Match +/− polarity and voltage rating to prevent electrolytic dielectric breakdown.
Voltmeter $R_V \gg R$ prevents parallel leakage current from shortening apparent $\tau$.

Determine the capacitance $C$ in μF (and note $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2$).
If the student repeats the discharge with a lower-impedance voltmeter of resistance 0.4 MΩ across the capacitor, calculate the reduced effective time constant $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
workingSteps: $R_{\mathrm{eff}} = (R R_V)/(R + R_V)$, giving $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = R_{\mathrm{eff}} C = 15.0 s$.

parts.prompt: Explain why electrolytic polarity must be checked and why $R_V \gg R$ is required.
parts.expectedAnswer: observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant
workingSteps: High voltmeter resistance prevents extra parallel discharge path lowering apparent RC.

items.stem: From a weather-station battery health audit, a student tabulates terminal p.d. 16.2 V at 0.8 A and 7.8 V at 3.6 A for the linear source shown. What is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (16.2 − 7.8)/(3.6 − 0.8) = 3.00 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 16.2 + (0.8)(3.00) = 18.6 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 18.6 V.

items.stem: In the chart-recorder range-attenuator network schematic, a 100 Ω–60 Ω potential divider across 14 V (ideal) is shunted across its 60 Ω lower arm by a 120 Ω load resistor. What current flows through the 120 Ω load branch?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (60 × 120)/(60 + 120) = 40.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 14 × 40.0 / (100 + 40.0) = 4.00 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 120 = 0.0333 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 120 = 0.133 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (40.0 Ω) to obtain 0.0333 A.

items.stem: The diagram shows a laboratory bridge module built from resistors whose values are multiples of R between terminals P and Q. The top branch contains 6R, and the lower branch consists of R in series with the parallel pair (6R || 12R) and another R. What is the total resistance between P and Q in terms of R?
items.workedSolution: Inner parallel pair: (6R × 12R) / (6R + 12R) = 4R. Lower branch total: R + 4R + R = 6R. Combining in parallel with 6R gives R_PQ = (6 × 6) / (6 + 6) R = 3R.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces the inner parallel pair, series lower branch, and outer parallel combination to obtain 3R.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a rail-weighbridge strain-strip divider: an ideal 6 V cell drives a 9 Ω resistor and 3.6 m of platinum-iridium wire R_1 (area 3.50 × 10⁻⁷ m², resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) in series.

markScheme.criterion: Applies R = ρL / A with given SI values.
Obtains R_1 = 2.57 Ω.
Adds 9 Ω to R_1 and divides 6 V by R_tot.
Obtains I = 0.519 A.
Multiplies I by R_1.
Obtains V_1 = 1.33 V.

items.stem: Two identical ideal cells, each of emf 12.0 V, are connected in parallel across a 20.0 Ω resistor in a marine navigation panel, as shown. What is the steady current supplied by each individual cell?
items.workedSolution: Identical ideal cells in parallel maintain terminal pd V = ε = 12.0 V (not 2ε). Main-branch current I = ε / R = 0.6000 A, and each cell supplies I/2 = 0.3000 A. Thus the answer is 0.300 A.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = ε for parallel identical cells to obtain 0.300 A.

items.stem: The $I\text{–}V$ characteristic of a silicon diode is shown. At the marked forward-bias operating point, $V = 0.780\text{ V}$ and $I = 0.0260\text{ A}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $R = 0.780 / 0.0260 = 30.0\,\Omega$. (b) conducts sharply above forward threshold potential difference with decreasing resistance while reverse bias has very high resistance; series resistor limits forward current.

Protective series resistor prevents excessive current / overheating in forward bias.

items.stem: A medium-wave radio receiver tuning stage uses a parallel LC tuned circuit with $L = 200\text{ }\mu\text{H}$, $C = 200\text{ pF}$, and quality factor $Q = 45$. At resonance the peak output voltage across the parallel LC network is $V_{\max} = 8.40 V$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_0 = 796 kHz$. (b) Half-power level $= 0.707 V_{\max} = 5.94 V$. (c) $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q = 17.7 kHz$. (d) Higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ with $\mu\text{H}$ and $\text{pF}$ converted to SI.
Obtains $f_0 = 796 kHz$.
Computes $0.707 V_{\max} = 5.94 V$.
Uses $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$.
Obtains $f_{\mathrm{B}} = 17.7 kHz$.
States higher Q improves selectivity against adjacent stations.
States narrower bandwidth can clip/attenuate outer modulating sidebands.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resonant frequency $f_0$ in kHz.
Calculate the voltage level at which the half-power bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ is measured on the resonance graph.
Calculate the bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ of the tuned circuit in kHz.
Explain the trade-off of replacing the coil with a lower-resistance coil to achieve a significantly higher Q factor in an AM broadcast receiver.
parts.expectedAnswer: A higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.
workingSteps: Higher Q sharpens the peak, improving selectivity against neighbouring stations.
However, $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$ shrinks, risking attenuation of high-frequency audio sidebands.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a primary lithium-manganese pack. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.500 A, V₁ = 6.08 V) and (I₂ = 1.70 A, V₂ = 4.82 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.450 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 25.0 mV when it carries 2.00 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 2.25 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 1.050 Ω ≈ 1.05 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 6.600 V ≈ 6.60 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01250 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 2.000 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 2.00 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0625 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 1.05 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 6.60 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0125 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 2.00 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0625 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 6.075 + 0.5 × 1.050 Ω = 6.600 V ≈ 6.60 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02500 V / 2.000 A = 0.01250 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: An optical-fibre receiver places a reverse-biased photodiode in series with a 100 kΩ resistor across a 10.0 V rail. When illuminated, the reverse photocurrent is 52.0 μA.
items.workedSolution: (a) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 5.20 V$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{D}} = 4.80 V$. (c) A reverse-biased photodiode produces a photocurrent directly proportional to incident light intensity.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $V = I_{\mathrm{p}} R$ with correct $\mu\text{A}$ and $\text{k}\Omega$ prefixes.
Obtains $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 5.20 V$.
Applies $V_{\mathrm{D}} = V_{\mathrm{s}} - V_{\mathrm{out}}$.
Obtains $V_{\mathrm{D}} = 4.80 V$.
States that photocurrent in reverse bias is directly proportional to light intensity.
Notes negligible dark current or faster response across the reverse-biased depletion layer.

parts.prompt: Calculate the output voltage developed across the sensing resistor.
Calculate the potential difference across the photodiode.
Explain why the photodiode is operated in reverse bias rather than forward bias for high-speed light sensing.
parts.expectedAnswer: A reverse-biased photodiode produces a photocurrent directly proportional to incident light intensity with a fast response.
workingSteps: In reverse bias, dark current is negligible and photogenerated carriers are swept rapidly across the wide depletion region.
Consequently, the reverse-biased photodiode produces a photocurrent directly proportional to incident light intensity.

items.stem: An ideal 24 V rail powers a blood-warmer safety cutoff divider containing a 230 Ω series resistor and an NTC thermistor (resistance 270 Ω, decreasing when heated). What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 270 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 230 + 270 = 500 Ω. Current I = 24 / 500 = 0.0480 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 24 × 270 / 500 = 13.0 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.622 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.622 W.

items.stem: In Required Practical 5, a student measures the resistance $R$ of varying lengths $L$ of a manganin alloy wire of mean diameter $(0.38 \pm 0.01)$ mm. The straight-line graph of $R$ against $L$ has gradient 3.9 Ω m⁻¹ ($\pm 2.4\%$) and vertical intercept 0.18 Ω.
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = 1.13 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. (b) $\rho = 4.42 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m$. (c) $\%\Delta\rho = 7.66\%$. (d) keep the current low and open the switch between readings to prevent wire heating while the non zero intercept represents contact and lead resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Converts diameter to metres and applies $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 1.13 × 10⁻⁷ m²$.
Uses $\rho = \mathrm{gradient} \times A$ (ignoring intercept).
Resistivity $\rho = 4.42 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m$.
Adds gradient percentage uncertainty to twice diameter percentage uncertainty.
Percentage uncertainty $= 7.66\%$.
Open switch / low current prevents Joule heating that would change wire temperature and $\rho$.
Positive intercept represents contact and connecting-lead resistance.

items.stem: In Required Practical 6, a student investigates a two-cell laboratory battery pack connected to a 3.3 Ω protective resistor and rheostat. Two well-spaced points on the straight best-fit graph of terminal potential difference $V$ against current $I$ are $(0.15\text{ A}, 2.91\text{ V})$ and $(0.55\text{ A}, 2.35\text{ V})$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $r = 1.40 Ω$. (b) $\varepsilon = 3.12 V$. (c) $I_{\max} = 0.664 A$. (d) include a protective series resistor and open the switch between readings to avoid heating the cell so internal resistance stays constant.

markScheme.criterion: Uses negative gradient of $V$ against $I$ line.
Internal resistance $r = 1.40 Ω$.
Substitutes point into $\varepsilon = V + Ir$.
Emf $\varepsilon = 3.12 V$.
Uses total resistance $r + R_{\mathrm{prot}}$ in $I = \varepsilon / R_{\mathrm{total}}$.
Maximum safe current $= 0.664 A$.
Protective resistor limits current to prevent short-circuit overheating.
Opening switch between readings prevents cell heating/draining so $r$ and $\varepsilon$ stay constant.

items.stem: Across a cryostat multi-channel heater block, a 2 Ω line resistor links an ideal 40.8 V rail to a three-way parallel manifold of 20 Ω, 30 Ω, and 60 Ω loads. What is the equivalent resistance of the three-branch parallel section (20 Ω, 30 Ω, and 60 Ω)?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/20 + 1/30 + 1/60, giving R_p = 10.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 2 + 10.0 = 12.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 40.8 / 12.0 = 3.40 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 34.0 V, and I(20 Ω) = V_p / 20 = 1.70 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 10.0 Ω.

items.stem: The circuit diagram shows a dc circuit verification board with two ideal cells of negligible internal resistance. Component values are ε₁ = 11.5 V, R₁ = 3.50 Ω, R₂ = 4.50 Ω, and R₃ = 6.50 Ω. The steady current in the bottom branch is measured as I₃ = 1.05 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Based on conservation of energy. (b) I₁ = 0.8469 A ≈ 0.847 A, so I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = 1.897 A ≈ 1.90 A. (c) ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 15.36 V ≈ 15.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: States conservation of energy.
Substitutes I₂ = I₁ + I₃ into ε₁ = I₁R₁ + I₂R₂ correctly.
Correct current I₁ = 0.847 A (and I₂ = 1.90 A).
Correctly evaluates middle-branch current I₂ = I₁ + I₃ and states ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Substitutes I₂R₂ and I₃R₃ consistently into the lower-loop equation.
Correct electromotive force ε₂ = 15.4 V.

parts.prompt: State the fundamental conservation law on which Kirchhoff's second law is based.
parts.expectedAnswer: Kirchhoff's second law is based on the conservation of energy.
workingSteps: Potential differences around a closed loop reflect electrical energy per unit charge.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's laws to the upper loop and junction Q to calculate the current I₁ in the upper branch (and hence find I₂).
workingSteps: At junction Q: I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = I₁ + 1.05 A.
Middle branch: I₂ = 0.8469 A + 1.050 A = 1.897 A ≈ 1.90 A.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's second law to the lower loop to determine the electromotive force ε₂.
workingSteps: State lower-loop equation: ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Calculate potential drop across R₂: I₂R₂ = 1.897 A × 4.5 = 8.536 V.
Add potential drop across R₃: ε₂ = 8.536 V + 6.825 V = 15.36 V ≈ 15.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ε / (R + r).

Uses V = ε − I r or V = I R_load.

Uses P = V I or I² R_load with external quantities.
Obtains P = 10.2 W.

items.workedSolution: (a) $G = 40.0$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = 12.5 V$. (c) Max unsaturated input $= 313 mV$. (d) Bandwidth $= \mathrm{GBP}/|G| = 60.0 kHz$.

Obtains $G = 40.0$.

Applies $V_{\mathrm{in,max}} = V_{\mathrm{sat}}/|G|$.
Obtains 313 mV.
Applies $\mathrm{BW} = \mathrm{GBP}/|G|$.
Obtains 60.0 kHz.

items.stem: A telemetry pulse-width clock module uses an RC astable timing circuit producing the waveforms shown, with $R_1 = 12.0 kΩ$, $R_2 = 48.0 kΩ$, and $C = 2.50 μF$. Its datasheet specifies $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$ and $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 105 ms$. (b) $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 84.0 ms$. (c) $\mathrm{PRF} = 1/(t_{\mathrm{H}} + t_{\mathrm{L}}) = 5.29 Hz$. (d) Duty cycle $= t_{\mathrm{H}}/T \times 100\% = 55.6\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$.
Obtains 105 ms.
Uses $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$.
Obtains 84.0 ms.
Sums $T = t_{\mathrm{H}} + t_{\mathrm{L}}$ in seconds and takes $1/T$.
Obtains 5.29 Hz.
Duty cycle $= 55.6\%$.

items.stem: In the high-resistance series loop shown, two ideal cells of electromotive forces ε₁ = 2.50 V and ε₂ = 6.50 V are connected in opposition in series with R₁ = 4.00 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. An ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 2.40 V. What is the resistance of R₂?
items.workedSolution: Since the positive terminals face each other, net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.000 V. Current I = V₁ / R₁ = 6.000 × 10⁻⁴ A. Potential difference across R₂ is V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.600 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 2.667 × 10³ Ω ≈ 2.67 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses opposing net emf ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.00 V to find R₂ = 2.67 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: During an RP9 charging experiment with a 9.0 V supply, a student plots ln(V₀ − V_C) against time t and obtains a straight line of gradient −0.03129 s⁻¹. Determine the RC time constant of the charging circuit.
items.workedSolution: Since ln(V₀ − V_C) = ln(V₀) − t/(RC), gradient = −1/(RC) → RC = 1 / 0.03129 = 32.0 s.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts time constant RC = 32.0 s.

items.stem: In Required Practical 9, a charged electrolytic capacitor discharges through a fixed resistor. Two points on the straight best-fit graph of $\ln(V / \mathrm{V})$ against $t$ are $(10\text{ s}, 1.745)$ and $(50\text{ s}, -0.066)$. Calculate the time constant $\tau = RC$.
items.workedSolution: Ideal time constant $\tau = RC = 22.1 s$, $C = 470$ μF, $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2 = 15.3 s$, and with parallel voltmeter $R_{\mathrm{eff}} = R R_V / (R + R_V)$, $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 21.1 s$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines timeConstantS $= 22.1 s$.

items.stem: In a solar-car sub-array V–I check (represented by the series resistance loop shown), a student measures a terminal p.d. of 19.6 V at 1.2 A; reducing the load resistance raises current to 4 A and lowers terminal p.d. to 12.6 V.

markScheme.criterion: Equates internal resistance to (V_1 − V_2) / (I_2 − I_1).

Substitutes r into ε = V + I r.
Obtains ε = 22.6 V.

items.stem: A conveyor-belt optical package counter uses an ideal 6 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 8 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 44 kΩ in darkness and 2.5 kΩ in bright light. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 44 + 8 = 52 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 52000 = 1.15 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.923 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 8 / (2.5 + 8) = 4.57 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.923 V.

items.stem: During a 25 s power-budget check on an industrial AGV safety-bumper and beacon bus, a battery (ε = 32.58 V, r = 2.1 Ω) energises a 6 Ω line resistor and parallel 15 Ω and 30 Ω branches.
items.workedSolution: (a) R_p = 10.0 Ω, R_tot = 18.1 Ω, I = 1.80 A. (b) P_source = ε I = 58.6 W. (c) V_term = 28.8 V, so E_ext = V_term I t = 1.30 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_tot including R_p, R_s, and r.
Obtains I = 1.80 A.
Applies P_source = ε I.
Obtains P_source = 58.6 W.
Finds terminal p.d. 28.8 V and multiplies by I and 25 s.
Obtains E_ext = 1.30 × 10³ J.

items.stem: In the foil strain-gauge conditioning loop schematic, R_1 is a 2 m strip of kanthal of cross-sectional area 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m² and resistivity 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, wired in series with 10 Ω across an ideal 8 V supply. What is the potential difference across the kanthal wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m)(2) / (5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 5.27 Ω. Series current I = 8 / (10 + 5.27) = 0.524 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 2.76 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 5.27 Ω and obtains 2.76 V.

items.stem: In the dual-cell heater load shown, two identical ideal cells of emf 6.00 V are wired in parallel across a 8.00 Ω resistor with an ideal ammeter A and voltmeter V.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = ε = 6.00 V, so I = ε / R = 0.750 A. (b) identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current.

markScheme.criterion: Correct ammeter reading 0.750 A.

workingSteps: For identical cells in parallel, V = ε = 6.00 V.

parts.prompt: Explain why connecting identical cells in parallel does not double the voltmeter reading.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because identical cells in parallel provide the same electromotive force as one cell while sharing the total current, the potential difference across both branches remains equal to the electromotive force of a single cell.
workingSteps: Each charge passes through only one cell on any closed loop, so parallel cells share current rather than adding energy per coulomb.

items.stem: To measure the full $I\text{–}V$ characteristic of a filament lamp smoothly down to $0\text{ V}$, how should the meters and variable supply be wired?
items.workedSolution: Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the component, the ammeter in series, and use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero. Therefore option D is correct: connect voltmeter in parallel across the component ammeter in series and use a potential divider to vary potential difference from zero.

items.stem: A parallel LC tuned circuit ($L = 400\text{ }\mu\text{H}$, $C = 250\text{ pF}$, $Q = 10.0$) has a symmetric voltage-response curve about its resonant frequency $f_0$. Calculate the lower half-power cut-off frequency $f_1$ (in kHz) where the output voltage drops to $0.707 V_{\max}$.
items.workedSolution: $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(400 \times 10^{-6})(250 \times 10^{-12})}} = 503 kHz$ and $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q = 50.3 kHz$. Hence $f_1 = f_0 - \frac{f_{\mathrm{B}}}{2} = 478 kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Lower half-power cut-off frequency equals 478 kHz.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reports the centre resonant frequency $f_0$ rather than subtracting $f_{\mathrm{B}}/2$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the full bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ instead of half the bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}/2$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds $f_{\mathrm{B}}/2$ to find the upper cut-off $f_2$ instead of the lower cut-off $f_1$.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a zinc-carbon lantern cell. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.300 A, V₁ = 4.14 V) and (I₂ = 1.30 A, V₂ = 2.94 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.400 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 24.0 mV when it carries 1.50 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 1.60 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 1.200 Ω ≈ 1.20 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 4.500 V ≈ 4.50 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01600 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 2.400 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 2.40 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0640 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 1.20 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 4.50 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0160 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 2.40 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0640 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 4.14 + 0.3 × 1.200 Ω = 4.500 V ≈ 4.50 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02400 V / 1.500 A = 0.01600 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: How must a Zener diode be connected in the voltage-reference circuit shown, and what feature of its $I$–$V$ characteristic produces a steady reference voltage $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$?
items.workedSolution: Connected with cathode K toward $+V_{\mathrm{s}}$ and anode A to $0\text{ V}$, a reverse-biased zener diode conducts steeply at its breakdown voltage maintaining a nearly constant reference potential across its terminals.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that reverse-biased zener diode conducts steeply at its breakdown voltage maintaining a nearly constant reference potential across its terminals.

options.label: A
options.text: Forward-biased Zener diode exhibits a linear ohmic gradient that doubles output potential with current.
options.distractorRationale: A forward-biased Zener diode conducts near $0.7\text{ V}$ like an ordinary silicon diode rather than at $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$.

options.label: B
options.text: Reverse-biased Zener diode blocks all current completely up to any supply voltage.
options.distractorRationale: Voltage-reference operation relies on controlled reverse breakdown conduction at $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$.

options.label: C
options.text: Reverse-biased zener diode conducts steeply at its breakdown voltage maintaining a nearly constant reference potential across its terminals.

options.label: D
options.text: Reverse-biased Zener diode increases its terminal potential linearly in proportion to reverse current.
options.distractorRationale: Its steep almost-vertical breakdown region keeps $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$ nearly constant as reverse current changes.

items.stem: During thermal calibration of a laser-diode TEC feedback divider, an ideal 14 V rail supplies a 150 Ω resistor in series with NTC thermistor R_1 (negative temperature coefficient). Steady p.d. across R_1 is measured by an ideal voltmeter as 8.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts 8.00 V from 14 V to find p.d. across 150 Ω.
Obtains I = 0.0400 A.
Divides V_NTC by the series current from (a).
Obtains R_1 = 200 Ω.
Uses P = V I or I² R_1.
Obtains P = 0.320 W.

items.stem: For a cryogenic sample-stage heater winding, technicians wind 3.6 m of 0.88 mm diameter kanthal wire (ρ = 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m) as resistor R_1 across an ideal 24 V supply. What steady current passes through R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.88 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 6.08 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 8.58 Ω. Current I = 24 / 8.58 = 2.80 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 67.1 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 2.80 A.

items.stem: During Required Practical 5, a constantan wire of mean diameter 0.32 mm is taped to a metre ruler. Plotting resistance $R$ against length $L$ produces a straight line of gradient 6.1 Ω m⁻¹ with a small positive vertical intercept 0.24 Ω. Calculate the resistivity $\rho$ of the alloy.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area $A = \pi (0.32 \times 10^{-3})^2 / 4 = 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m²$. Resistivity $\rho = \mathrm{gradient} \times A = 4.91 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta\rho = 2 + 2(3.13) = 8.25\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines resistivityRho $= 4.91 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m$.

items.stem: Why does the standard AQA Required Practical 6 circuit include a fixed protective series resistor alongside the variable resistor and a switch opened between readings?
items.workedSolution: RP6 mark-scheme explanation: Include a protective series resistor and open the switch between readings to avoid heating the cell so internal resistance stays constant.

markScheme.criterion: Include a protective series resistor and open the switch between readings to avoid heating the cell so internal resistance stays constant.

options.label: A
options.text: The protective resistor increases the short-circuit current so the voltmeter spans a wider voltage range.
options.distractorRationale: The protective resistor limits maximum current to prevent overheating and cell drain.

options.label: B
options.text: The protective resistor increases the measured internal resistance r directly on the V against I graph.
options.distractorRationale: Because the voltmeter sits across the cell terminals only, external resistors do not change the slope −r.

options.label: C
options.text: Include a protective series resistor and open the switch between readings to avoid heating the cell so internal resistance stays constant.

options.label: D
options.text: Leaving the switch permanently closed warms the cell to its steady maximum emf.
options.distractorRationale: Continuous current discharges and heats the cell, causing ε and r to drift during the practical.

items.stem: A series divider in an audio preamp bias-point check has a 120 Ω upper arm and 400 Ω lower arm across an ideal 45 V source. Connecting a non-ideal 1200 Ω voltmeter across the 400 Ω arm (forming the parallel pair shown) yields what potential difference?
items.workedSolution: The 1200 Ω voltmeter shunts the 400 Ω resistor: R_p = (400 × 1200)/(400 + 1200) = 300 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 45 × 300 / (120 + 300) = 32.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 400 Ω and 1200 Ω in parallel (300 Ω) to obtain V = 32.1 V.

items.stem: A weighted 3-bit digital-to-analogue summing amplifier ($\pm 12.5 V$ rails) has $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 50\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_1 = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_2 = 25\text{ k}\Omega$, and $R_3 = 50\text{ k}\Omega$. The inputs are set to $V_1 = 2.00 V$, $V_2 = 1.50 V$, and $V_3 = 1.00 V$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I_{\mathrm{tot}} = 0.280 mA$. (b) $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −12.5 V$. (c) Virtual earth holds the summing junction at zero volts so each input branch current depends only on its own voltage and resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Sums $V_1/R_1 + V_2/R_2 + V_3/R_3$ using virtual earth at node X.
Obtains 0.280 mA.
Computes $-I_{\mathrm{tot}} R_{\mathrm{f}}$ and compares with $\pm V_{\mathrm{sat}}$.
Obtains $V_{\mathrm{out}} = −12.5 V$.
States that node X is held at $0\text{ V}$ (virtual earth) while unsaturated.
Concludes each branch current $V_k/R_k$ is independent of the other inputs.

parts.prompt: Explain why changing one input voltage does not alter the currents in the other input branches while the amplifier stays unsaturated.
parts.expectedAnswer: Virtual earth holds the summing junction at zero volts so each input branch current depends only on its own voltage and resistor.
workingSteps: Because open-loop gain is very large and the amplifier is unsaturated, node X stays at $0\text{ V}$.
Each branch current $V_k/R_k$ is therefore fixed purely by its own input voltage and resistor with zero crosstalk.

items.stem: In the schematic of a microgrid load-shedding relay bank, an ideal 9 V supply feeds a 3 Ω series resistor that branches at a node into parallel 18 Ω, 36 Ω, and 12 Ω resistors.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3 and inverts.
Obtains R_p = 6.00 Ω.
Adds 3 Ω to R_p and uses I = V / R_tot.
Obtains I_tot = 1.00 A.
Calculates V_p = 6.00 V and divides by 18 Ω.
Obtains I_1 = 0.333 A.

items.stem: A 2 m kanthal wire R_1 of area 3.50 × 10⁻⁷ m² and resistivity 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m is shunted by a 7 Ω resistor in a battery-cycler current-sense shunt network behind a 6 Ω series ballast across 21 V (ideal). What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 7 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 8.29 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 7)/(R_1 + 7) = 3.79 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 6 + 3.79 = 9.79 Ω; main current I_tot = 2.14 A, V_p = 8.14 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 0.982 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 8.29 Ω and obtains 3.79 Ω.

items.stem: In the laboratory Kirchhoff network shown, both cells have negligible internal resistance, with ε₁ = 9.00 V, R₁ = 3.00 Ω, R₂ = 4.50 Ω, and R₃ = 6.00 Ω. Given that the current in the lower branch is I₃ = 0.600 A, calculate the electromotive force ε₂ of the lower cell.
items.workedSolution: At junction Q, Kirchhoff's first law gives I₂ = I₁ + I₃. Around the upper loop, ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₂R₂ = 0, so I₁ = (ε₁ − I₃R₂) / (R₁ + R₂) = 0.8400 A and I₂ = 1.440 A. Around the lower loop, ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 10.08 V. Hence the required answer is 10.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's first and second laws to obtain 10.1 V.

items.stem: The circuit models a weather-buoy primary lithium cell as an ideal 18.26 V source in series with 1.3 Ω internal resistance driving a 7 Ω load. What power is dissipated in the 7 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 18.26 / (7 + 1.3) = 2.20 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 18.26 − (2.20)(1.3) = 15.4 V. External load power P = I² R = 33.9 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 33.9 W.

items.stem: An audio engineer increases the feedback resistor $R_{\mathrm{f}}$ of a real op-amp stage to boost voltage gain while leaving the op-amp IC unchanged. How does this alter the frequency response?
items.workedSolution: Because $G \times \mathrm{BW} = \mathrm{GBP} = \text{constant}$, increasing closed-loop voltage gain reduces available bandwidth because gain times bandwidth is constant.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that increasing closed-loop voltage gain reduces available bandwidth because gain times bandwidth is constant.

items.stem: An industrial turbine shaft carries $6$ evenly spaced magnets past a Hall effect tachometer probe, producing $240\text{ pulses s}^{-1}$. What is the turbine speed in $\text{rev min}^{-1}$?
items.workedSolution: Revolutions per second $= 240 / 6 = 40.0\text{ Hz}$, so speed $= 40.0 \times 60 = 2.40 × 10³ rev min⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 2.40 × 10³ rev min⁻¹.

items.stem: An RC astable oscillator uses $R_1 = 36.0\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_2 = 18.0\text{ k}\Omega$, and capacitor $C$, with datasheet timing equations $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$ and $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$. Calculate its mark-to-space ratio $t_{\mathrm{H}} / t_{\mathrm{L}}$.
items.workedSolution: The factor $0.7 C$ cancels: $\frac{t_{\mathrm{H}}}{t_{\mathrm{L}}} = \frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_2} = \frac{36.0 + 18.0}{18.0} = 3.00$.

markScheme.criterion: Mark-to-space ratio equals 3.00.

parts.prompt: Calculate the circuit current and hence determine the resistance of R₂.
workingSteps: Opposing cells give net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.000 V.
Series current I = V₁ / R₁ = 2.4 / 1600 = 1.500 × 10⁻³ A.
Potential difference V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.600 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 1.067 × 10³ Ω ≈ 1.07 × 10³ Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy dissipated in resistor R₁ during the 4 min interval.

items.stem: In the laboratory oil-bath immersion coil diagram, a cell (ε = 26.75 V, r = 1.9 Ω) supplies a 19.5 Ω external resistor steadily for 75 s. What total energy is delivered to the 19.5 Ω resistor?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 26.75 / (19.5 + 1.9) = 1.25 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 24.4 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 2.29 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 1.25 A and E_ext = I² R t = 2.29 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A laboratory counter-emf motor stand-in loop pairs a 15 V driver cell of internal resistance 1 Ω in series opposition with a 3 V counter-cell of internal resistance 0.7 Ω (drawn as net ε, r) across 9 Ω and 14 Ω resistors. What is the potential difference across the 14 Ω load resistor?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 15 − 3 = 12 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 1 + 0.7 + 9 + 14 = 24.7 Ω. Loop current I = 12 / 24.7 = 0.486 A. Load p.d. V = 6.80 V and load power P = 3.30 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 6.80 V.

items.stem: In AQA Required Practical 5 (determining the resistivity of a wire), which meter arrangement and measurement precaution produce an accurate resistivity value?
items.workedSolution: Series ammeter + parallel voltmeter give R = V/I, a low current avoids temperature rise, and perpendicular micrometer checks detect non-uniform cross-section. Therefore the correct statement is: As shown in the RP5 schematic, connect the ammeter in series and the high-resistance voltmeter in parallel across the measured wire length, keep the current low to avoid heating, and measure wire diameter in perpendicular directions with a micrometer.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: connect the ammeter in series and the high-resistance voltmeter in parallel across the measured wire length, keep the current low to avoid heating, and measure wire diameter in perpendicular directions with a micrometer.

items.stem: In Required Practical 9, a charged electrolytic capacitor discharges through a 68 kΩ resistor. Two points on the straight best-fit line of $\ln(V / \mathrm{V})$ against $t$ are $(20\text{ s}, 1.359)$ and $(100\text{ s}, -0.371)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\tau = 46.2 s$ ($T_{1/2} = 32.1 s$). (b) $C = 680 μF$. (c) $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 43.8 s$. (d) observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

markScheme.criterion: Computes negative gradient of $\ln V$ vs $t$ and equates to $-1/\tau$.
Time constant $\tau = 46.2 s$.
Uses $C = \tau / R$ with $R$ in Ω.
Capacitance $C = 680 μF$.
Combines $R$ and $R_V$ in parallel: $1/R_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1/R + 1/R_V$.
Effective time constant $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 43.8 s$.
Match +/− polarity and voltage rating to prevent electrolytic dielectric breakdown.
Voltmeter $R_V \gg R$ prevents parallel leakage current from shortening apparent $\tau$.

Determine the capacitance $C$ in μF (and note $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2$).

items.stem: During an electrochemical cell coursework investigation (modelled by source V with internal and load resistances R in series), terminal p.d. is 21.9 V at current 1 A and drops to 17.4 V when current increases to 3 A. What is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (21.9 − 17.4)/(3 − 1) = 2.25 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 21.9 + (1)(2.25) = 24.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 24.1 V.

items.stem: A pressure-transducer excitation divider uses 55 Ω and 75 Ω divider resistors across an ideal 13 V DC source, with a 150 Ω external load wired in parallel across the 75 Ω arm as shown. What electrical power is delivered to the 150 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (75 × 150)/(75 + 150) = 50.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 13 × 50.0 / (55 + 50.0) = 6.19 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 150 = 0.0413 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 150 = 0.255 W.

items.stem: The diagram shows a compact passive network built from resistors whose values are multiples of R between terminals P and Q. The top branch contains 6R, and the lower branch consists of R in series with the parallel pair (2R || 2R) and another R. What is the total resistance between P and Q in terms of R?
items.workedSolution: Inner parallel pair: (2R × 2R) / (2R + 2R) = 1R. Lower branch total: R + 1R + R = 3R. Combining in parallel with 6R gives R_PQ = (6 × 3) / (6 + 3) R = 2R.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces the inner parallel pair, series lower branch, and outer parallel combination to obtain 2R.

items.stem: A cleanroom UV-lamp verification sensor connects an LDR in series with a 8 kΩ fixed resistor across an ideal 12 V DC source, with ideal voltmeter Vout connected across the 8 kΩ resistor as shown. The LDR resistance is 102 kΩ in darkness and 0.5 kΩ in bright light.

Multiplies I_dark by R_fixed or applies divider formula.

Uses bright LDR resistance 0.5 kΩ in potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_out(bright) = 11.3 V.

items.stem: The diagram illustrates a piezoresistive alloy-ribbon test loop where an ideal 26 V rail supplies a 7 Ω resistor in series with uniform stainless-steel wire R_1 (L = 5.6 m, A = 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m).

markScheme.criterion: Applies R = ρL / A with given SI values.
Obtains R_1 = 13.4 Ω.

Obtains I = 1.27 A.
Multiplies I by R_1.
Obtains V_1 = 17.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 12.0 Ω and adds 14 Ω.

Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 18.
Obtains P = 50.0 W.

items.stem: Two identical ideal cells, each of emf 4.50 V, are connected in parallel across a 9.00 Ω resistor in an emergency beacon circuit, as shown. What is the steady current supplied by each individual cell?
items.workedSolution: Identical ideal cells in parallel maintain terminal pd V = ε = 4.50 V (not 2ε). Main-branch current I = ε / R = 0.5000 A, and each cell supplies I/2 = 0.2500 A. Thus the answer is 0.250 A.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = ε for parallel identical cells to obtain 0.250 A.

items.stem: A $12.0\text{ V}$ car headlamp bulb draws a steady current of $0.800\text{ A}$ at its marked operating point on the $I\text{–}V$ curve shown alongside its test circuit.
items.workedSolution: (a) $R = 12.0/0.800 = 15.0\,\Omega$, $P = 9.60\text{ W}$. (b) Resistance is V divided by I filament ions vibrate more with temperature while thermistor carrier density rises sharply; explains cold switch-on surge current, filament vs NTC physics, and $R = V/I \ne 1/\text{gradient}$.

markScheme.criterion: Resistance $= 15.0\,\Omega$.
Power $P = VI = 9.60\text{ W}$.
L1 (Area 1): When cold at switch-on, lattice vibrations are smaller so filament resistance is much lower than at operating temperature.
L1 (Area 1): Low initial resistance causes a large initial surge current (I = V/R) and intense local heating at thin spots, blowing the filament.
L2 (Area 2): As filament heats up, positive lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude causing more frequent collisions with conduction electrons so R rises.
L2 (Area 2): In contrast, heating an NTC thermistor liberates many more free charge carriers (n rises sharply), dominating over lattice vibrations so R falls.
L3 (Area 3): Resistance at any operating point is strictly defined as R = V/I (ratio of coordinate values).
L3 (Area 3): Explains 1/gradient measures tangent dV/dI which only equals V/I for a straight line through the origin (ohmic conductor).
