parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical resistance and power dissipation of the headlamp filament at this operating point.

Explain why the headlamp filament is most likely to blow at the instant it is switched on from cold, contrast its resistance–temperature physics with an NTC thermistor, and explain why taking $1/\text{gradient}$ gives the wrong resistance on both curves.
parts.expectedAnswer: Resistance is V divided by I filament ions vibrate more with temperature while thermistor carrier density rises sharply. When cold at switch-on, lattice ion vibration amplitude is small so collisions with conduction electrons are less frequent and filament resistance is much lower than when hot; applying full $12\text{ V}$ therefore produces a large initial surge current ($I = V/R$) and rapid local heating at thin spots, making failure most likely at switch-on. As temperature rises, larger lattice vibrations increase collisions and raise $R$ (opposite to an NTC thermistor where rising temperature liberates far more free charge carriers, outweighing vibrations and reducing $R$). Because both curves are non-linear, resistance is defined by the chord ratio $R = V/I$ to the origin, whereas $1/\text{gradient}$ equals the differential ratio $dV/dI \ne V/I$.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Cold filament has small lattice vibration -> low resistance -> large surge current I = V/R at switch-on -> rapid heating/failure.
Area 2 (L2): Hot filament lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude -> more electron collisions -> higher R; contrast with NTC carrier density n increase lowering R.
Area 3 (L3): Explain strictly why R = V/I (ratio of coordinates) differs from 1/gradient (dV/dI) on curved I-V graphs.

items.stem: A long-wave meteorological station tuner uses a parallel LC tuned circuit with $L = 500\text{ }\mu\text{H}$, $C = 125\text{ pF}$, and quality factor $Q = 64$. At resonance the peak output voltage across the parallel LC network is $V_{\max} = 11.0 V$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_0 = 637 kHz$. (b) Half-power level $= 0.707 V_{\max} = 7.78 V$. (c) $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q = 9.95 kHz$. (d) Higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ with $\mu\text{H}$ and $\text{pF}$ converted to SI.
Obtains $f_0 = 637 kHz$.
Computes $0.707 V_{\max} = 7.78 V$.
Uses $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$.
Obtains $f_{\mathrm{B}} = 9.95 kHz$.
States higher Q improves selectivity against adjacent stations.
States narrower bandwidth can clip/attenuate outer modulating sidebands.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resonant frequency $f_0$ in kHz.
Calculate the voltage level at which the half-power bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ is measured on the resonance graph.
Calculate the bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ of the tuned circuit in kHz.
Explain the trade-off of replacing the coil with a lower-resistance coil to achieve a significantly higher Q factor in an AM broadcast receiver.
parts.expectedAnswer: A higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.
workingSteps: Higher Q sharpens the peak, improving selectivity against neighbouring stations.
However, $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$ shrinks, risking attenuation of high-frequency audio sidebands.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a field-station battery unit. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.400 A, V₁ = 5.06 V) and (I₂ = 1.80 A, V₂ = 3.87 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.600 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 9.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 29.0 mV when it carries 2.40 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 3.00 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 0.8500 Ω ≈ 0.850 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 5.400 V ≈ 5.40 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01208 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.913 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.91 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0604 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 0.850 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 5.40 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0121 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.91 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0604 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 5.06 + 0.4 × 0.8500 Ω = 5.400 V ≈ 5.40 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02900 V / 2.400 A = 0.01208 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: An electronics engineer uses the reverse-biased Zener diode circuit and $I$–$V$ characteristic shown to generate a fixed reference voltage $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$ for an analogue comparator from a battery pack whose voltage varies between 11 V and 15 V.
items.workedSolution: In forward bias it conducts near 0.7 V; in reverse bias (cathode to $+V_{\mathrm{s}}$ via $R_{\mathrm{s}}$, anode to $0\text{ V}$) a reverse-biased zener diode conducts steeply at its breakdown voltage maintaining a nearly constant reference potential across its terminals. Supply changes are dropped across $R_{\mathrm{s}}$; $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ is bounded above by $I_{\mathrm{Z}} \ge I_{\mathrm{Z,min}}$ at $11\text{ V}$ and bounded below by $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z,max}} \le P_{\max}$ at $15\text{ V}$.

markScheme.criterion: Describes forward-bias conduction near $0.7\text{ V}$ and reverse-bias blocking up to sharp vertical breakdown at $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$.
Correctly identifies reverse-bias orientation: cathode K towards $+V_{\mathrm{s}}$ via $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ and anode A to $0\text{ V}$.
Explains that the nearly vertical reverse-breakdown characteristic keeps $V_{\mathrm{ref}} \approx V_{\mathrm{Z}}$ despite current changes.
Explains that variations in battery supply voltage are dropped across the series resistor $R_{\mathrm{s}}$.
Shows $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ must be small enough at lowest $V_{\mathrm{s}}$ so reverse current stays above $I_{\mathrm{Z,min}}$.
Shows $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ must be large enough at highest $V_{\mathrm{s}}$ so $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z,max}}$ stays below the diode power rating $P_{\max}$.

parts.prompt: Explain the shape of the Zener diode $I$–$V$ characteristic in both forward and reverse bias, how the anode and cathode must be biased to produce $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$, and how the series current-limiting resistor $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ is chosen using the minimum breakdown current $I_{\mathrm{Z,min}}$ and maximum power rating $P_{\max}$.
parts.expectedAnswer: In forward bias, the Zener diode behaves like an ordinary silicon diode and conducts sharply above about 0.7 V; in reverse bias it blocks current until the breakdown voltage $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$ is reached, where a reverse-biased zener diode conducts steeply at its breakdown voltage maintaining a nearly constant reference potential across its terminals. To produce a positive reference voltage $V_{\mathrm{ref}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}}$, the cathode K must be connected via the series resistor $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ to the positive supply rail and the anode A to 0 V. When the battery supply voltage varies between 11 V and 15 V, changes in supply potential are absorbed as changes in the voltage drop $V_{\mathrm{s}} - V_{\mathrm{Z}}$ across $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ while $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$ remains almost constant. To keep the diode firmly on the vertical breakdown region even at the lowest supply voltage (11 V), $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ must not exceed $(V_{\mathrm{s,min}} - V_{\mathrm{Z}})/I_{\mathrm{Z,min}}$. Conversely, at the highest supply voltage (15 V), $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ must be large enough that the reverse current $I_{\mathrm{Z,max}} = (V_{\mathrm{s,max}} - V_{\mathrm{Z}})/R_{\mathrm{s}}$ keeps power dissipation $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z,max}}$ safely below the maximum power rating $P_{\max}$.
workingSteps: L1: Describe forward bias ($\approx 0.7\text{ V}$ conduction threshold like a standard silicon diode) and reverse bias (negligible current until sharp vertical breakdown at $-V_{\mathrm{Z}}$).
L1: State correct reverse-bias orientation: cathode K towards $+V_{\mathrm{s}}$ via $R_{\mathrm{s}}$, anode A connected to $0\text{ V}$.
L2: Explain that on the steep reverse-breakdown knee, a large change in reverse current produces almost no change in $V_{\mathrm{Z}}$, holding $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$ steady.
L2: Explain that supply voltage fluctuations alter the potential drop across $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ rather than $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$.
L3: Derive upper bound on $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ from minimum supply voltage so $I_{\mathrm{Z}} \ge I_{\mathrm{Z,min}}$.
L3: Derive lower bound on $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ from maximum supply voltage so $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z,max}} \le P_{\max}$ to prevent thermal damage.

items.stem: The divider stage of a PCR thermal-cycler block sensor wires a 330 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 770 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 24 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 770 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 330 + 770 = 1100 Ω. Current I = 24 / 1100 = 0.0218 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 24 × 770 / 1100 = 16.8 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.367 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.367 W.

items.stem: In Required Practical 5, the diameter of a manganin alloy wire is measured as $(0.38 \pm 0.01)$ mm and the gradient of the $R$ against $L$ graph has percentage uncertainty 2.4%. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in resistivity $\rho$.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area $A = \pi (0.38 \times 10^{-3})^2 / 4 = 1.13 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. Resistivity $\rho = \mathrm{gradient} \times A = 4.42 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta\rho = 2.4 + 2(2.63) = 7.66\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines pctUncRho $= 7.66\%$.

items.stem: In Required Practical 6 on a zinc-carbon dry cell, two points on the best-fit straight line of terminal potential difference $V$ against current $I$ are $(0.12\text{ A}, 1.46\text{ V})$ and $(0.44\text{ A}, 1.19\text{ V})$. Determine the internal resistance $r$ of the cell.
items.workedSolution: From $V = \varepsilon - Ir$, gradient $-r = (1.19 - 1.46)/(0.44 - 0.12) = -0.85$ Ω, $\varepsilon = 1.56$ V, and $I_{\max} = \varepsilon/(r + R_{\mathrm{prot}}) = 0.511 A$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines internalResistanceR $= 0.850 Ω$.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains R_p = 750 Ω.

Obtains I = 0.0304 A.
Multiplies supply current by R_p (or uses loaded divider ratio).
Obtains V_meter = 22.8 V.

items.stem: Why is a balanced difference amplifier superior to a standard non-inverting amplifier when amplifying millivolt signals from a remote strain gauge connected via long parallel cables?
items.workedSolution: Because $V_{\mathrm{out}} = (V_+ - V_-)R_{\mathrm{f}}/R_1$, equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that equal noise induced on both sensor leads cancels when subtracted by a balanced difference amplifier.

items.stem: Three resistors of 14 Ω, 21 Ω, and 42 Ω are wired in parallel inside a marine navigation beacon board and fed through a 5 Ω resistor from an ideal 36 V DC source. What is the equivalent resistance of the three-branch parallel section (14 Ω, 21 Ω, and 42 Ω)?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/14 + 1/21 + 1/42, giving R_p = 7.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 5 + 7.00 = 12.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 36 / 12.0 = 3.00 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 21.0 V, and I(14 Ω) = V_p / 14 = 1.50 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 7.00 Ω.

items.stem: During testing of a wind-tunnel sting-heater shunt loop, 2 m of platinum-iridium wire R_1 (cross-sectional area 4.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) is wired in parallel with 14 Ω and supplied via 5 Ω from an ideal 31 V rail.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 1.25 Ω and combines in parallel with 14 Ω.
Obtains R_p = 1.15 Ω.
Adds 5 Ω to R_p and uses I = V / R_tot.
Obtains I_tot = 5.04 A.
Finds V_p and uses P_1 = V_p² / R_1.
Obtains P_1 = 26.8 W.

items.stem: The circuit diagram shows a low-voltage junction board with two ideal cells of negligible internal resistance. Component values are ε₁ = 9.50 V, R₁ = 2.00 Ω, R₂ = 6.00 Ω, and R₃ = 4.00 Ω. The steady current in the bottom branch is measured as I₃ = 0.750 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Based on conservation of energy. (b) I₁ = 0.6250 A ≈ 0.625 A, so I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = 1.375 A ≈ 1.38 A. (c) ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 11.25 V ≈ 11.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: States conservation of energy.
Substitutes I₂ = I₁ + I₃ into ε₁ = I₁R₁ + I₂R₂ correctly.
Correct current I₁ = 0.625 A (and I₂ = 1.38 A).
Correctly evaluates middle-branch current I₂ = I₁ + I₃ and states ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Substitutes I₂R₂ and I₃R₃ consistently into the lower-loop equation.
Correct electromotive force ε₂ = 11.3 V.

parts.prompt: State the fundamental conservation law on which Kirchhoff's second law is based.
parts.expectedAnswer: Kirchhoff's second law is based on the conservation of energy.
workingSteps: Potential differences around a closed loop reflect electrical energy per unit charge.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's laws to the upper loop and junction Q to calculate the current I₁ in the upper branch (and hence find I₂).
workingSteps: At junction Q: I₂ = I₁ + I₃ = I₁ + 0.750 A.
Middle branch: I₂ = 0.6250 A + 0.7500 A = 1.375 A ≈ 1.38 A.

parts.prompt: Apply Kirchhoff's second law to the lower loop to determine the electromotive force ε₂.
workingSteps: State lower-loop equation: ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃.
Calculate potential drop across R₂: I₂R₂ = 1.375 A × 6 = 8.250 V.
Add potential drop across R₃: ε₂ = 8.250 V + 3.000 V = 11.25 V ≈ 11.3 V.

items.stem: An inverting op-amp powered by $\pm 13.0\text{ V}$ saturation rails uses $R_{\mathrm{in}} = 12.0\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 150\text{ k}\Omega$. When an input potential of $+400\text{ mV}$ is applied, calculate the output voltage $V_{\mathrm{out}}$.
items.workedSolution: Closed-loop gain $G = -\frac{R_{\mathrm{f}}}{R_{\mathrm{in}}} = -\frac{150}{12.0} = -12.5$. Hence $V_{\mathrm{out}} = -12.5 \times 0.400\text{ V} = −5.00 V$, which lies safely within $\pm 13.0\text{ V}$.

markScheme.criterion: Output voltage equals −5.00 V.

items.stem: How does a set of orthogonal Hall effect sensors monitor the attitude (pitch, roll, and yaw orientation) of a small satellite or autonomous craft?
items.workedSolution: Because output varies with $\cos\theta$ relative to the ambient field, a Hall sensor measures magnetic field alignment to monitor vehicle or spacecraft attitude.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that Hall sensor measures magnetic field alignment to monitor vehicle or spacecraft attitude.

items.stem: In the two-cell diagnostic circuit shown, two ideal cells of electromotive forces ε₁ = 1.60 V and ε₂ = 5.20 V are connected in opposition in series with R₁ = 1.80 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. An ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 2.10 V. What is the resistance of R₂?
items.workedSolution: Since the positive terminals face each other, net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 3.600 V. Current I = V₁ / R₁ = 1.167 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across R₂ is V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.500 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 1.286 × 10³ Ω ≈ 1.29 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses opposing net emf ε₂ − ε₁ = 3.60 V to find R₂ = 1.29 × 10³ Ω.

options.label: A
options.text: A straight line of gradient −1/(RC) confirms exponential decay; to preserve safety and accuracy, observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

options.label: B
options.text: Plotting V against 1/t produces a straight line of gradient RC.
options.distractorRationale: Exponential decay V = V₀ e^(−t/RC) linearizes via ln V vs t, not V vs 1/t.

options.label: C
options.text: The vertical intercept of ln V vs t equals V₀ directly without taking exp.
options.distractorRationale: The vertical intercept at t = 0 equals ln V₀, so V₀ = e^c.

options.label: D
options.text: Using a very small resistor R (10 Ω) gives a slow discharge that is easy to read manually.
options.distractorRationale: A small R makes τ = RC tiny (milliseconds), requiring a data-logger; choose R so τ ≈ 20–60 s for manual timing.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a photographic darkroom door interlock connects an LDR (61 kΩ in darkness, 0.8 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 8 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 61 + 8 = 69 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 69000 = 1.74 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.39 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 8 / (0.8 + 8) = 10.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 10.9 V.

items.workedSolution: (a) R_p = 12.0 Ω, R_tot = 24.3 Ω, I = 2.00 A. (b) P_source = ε I = 97.2 W. (c) V_term = 46.0 V, so E_ext = V_term I t = 9.20 × 10³ J.

Obtains E_ext = 9.20 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A slide-wire potentiometer rail places a 5 Ω reference resistor in series with a uniform stainless-steel wire R_1 (resistivity 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 4.4 m, area 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) across an ideal 17 V DC source, as shown. What is the potential difference across the stainless-steel wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m)(4.4) / (3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 10.6 Ω. Series current I = 17 / (5 + 10.6) = 1.09 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 11.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 10.6 Ω and obtains 11.5 V.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω inside a cryogenic transfer-line warm-up harness receive current through a 15 Ω series resistor from an ideal 43.2 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 12 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 15 + 3.00 = 18.0 Ω. Supply current I = 43.2 / 18.0 = 2.40 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 2.40 × 3.00 = 7.20 V. Power in 12 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 12 = 4.32 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 7.20 V and calculates P = 4.32 W.

items.stem: Two identical ideal cells, each of emf 3.60 V, are connected in parallel to drive a 12.0 Ω load in a lithium-ion parallel module. What reading is shown on the ideal ammeter A in the main branch?
items.workedSolution: Identical ideal cells in parallel maintain terminal pd V = ε = 3.60 V (not 2ε). Main-branch current I = ε / R = 0.3000 A, and each cell supplies I/2 = 0.1500 A. Thus the answer is 0.300 A.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = ε for parallel identical cells to obtain 0.300 A.

items.stem: Unlike a metal filament, an NTC semiconductor thermistor exhibits an $I\text{–}V$ curve that bends upwards as current and temperature rise. What microscopic process dominates?
items.workedSolution: In an NTC semiconductor, higher temperature liberates many more free charge carriers, outweighing increased lattice vibrations so resistance decreases. Therefore option A is correct: higher temperature liberates many more free charge carriers outweighing lattice vibrations so resistance decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: higher temperature liberates many more free charge carriers outweighing lattice vibrations so resistance decreases.

items.stem: A battery of emf 13.6 V and internal resistance 3 Ω powers an off-grid cabin DC lighting and pump bus made of a 4 Ω series resistor and parallel 15 Ω and 30 Ω branches, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 90 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (15 × 30)/(15 + 30) = 10.0 Ω, R_ext = 4 + 10.0 = 14.0 Ω, and R_tot = 14.0 + 3 = 17.0 Ω. Current I = 13.6 / 17.0 = 0.800 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 13.6 − (0.800)(3) = 11.2 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 806 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 806 J.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a three-cell chemistry battery. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.500 A, V₁ = 4.35 V) and (I₂ = 1.50 A, V₂ = 3.45 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.600 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 7.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 36.0 mV when it carries 2.50 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 3.00 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 0.9000 Ω ≈ 0.900 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 4.800 V ≈ 4.80 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01440 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.800 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.80 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0720 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 0.900 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 4.80 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0144 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.80 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0720 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 4.35 + 0.5 × 0.9000 Ω = 4.800 V ≈ 4.80 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.03600 V / 2.500 A = 0.01440 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: A 6.2 V Zener diode is connected in reverse bias through a 200 Ω series current-limiting resistor across a 15.0 V DC supply to provide a reference potential to a high-resistance circuit node (negligible output current). Calculate the electrical power dissipated in the Zener diode.
items.workedSolution: The reverse current through $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ and the Zener diode is $I_{\mathrm{Z}} = \frac{15.0 - 6.2}{200} = 44.0\text{ mA}$. Hence the Zener power dissipation is $P_{\mathrm{Z}} = V_{\mathrm{Z}} I_{\mathrm{Z}} = 6.2 \times 44.0\text{ mA} = 273 mW$.

markScheme.criterion: Zener diode power dissipation equals 273 mW.

items.stem: Across an ideal 18 V terminal pair in a wind-tunnel hot-wire anemometer probe, resistor R_1 consists of 3.6 m of cylindrical stainless-steel wire having diameter 0.82 mm and resistivity 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. What is the electrical resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.82 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 5.28 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 4.91 Ω. Current I = 18 / 4.91 = 3.67 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 66.0 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 4.91 Ω.

items.stem: On a strain-bridge balance verification rig, resistors of 30 Ω and 180 Ω form a series divider across an ideal 34 V DC supply. A finite-resistance voltmeter (90 Ω, drawn as the parallel branch) is placed across the 180 Ω resistor. What reading does the voltmeter show?
items.workedSolution: The 90 Ω voltmeter shunts the 180 Ω resistor: R_p = (180 × 90)/(180 + 90) = 60.0 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 34 × 60.0 / (30 + 60.0) = 22.7 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 180 Ω and 90 Ω in parallel (60.0 Ω) to obtain V = 22.7 V.

items.stem: In a multi-channel summing amplifier audio mixer, why does adjusting the volume slider on Channel 1 cause zero crosstalk or interference into Channel 2?
items.workedSolution: Because the op-amp is unsaturated, virtual earth holds the summing junction at zero volts so each input branch current depends only on its own voltage and resistor ($I_k = V_k/R_k$), isolating the inputs from one another.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that virtual earth holds the summing junction at zero volts so each input branch current depends only on its own voltage and resistor.

items.stem: Refer to a magnet-power-supply trim-shunt stage shown: parallel arms R_1 (titanium, length 6.5 m, area 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and 15 Ω connect through 8 Ω to an ideal 21 V rail. What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 15 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 5.46 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 15)/(R_1 + 15) = 4.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 8 + 4.00 = 12.0 Ω; main current I_tot = 1.75 A, V_p = 7.00 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 1.28 A.

items.stem: In the two-branch student rig shown, both cells have negligible internal resistance, with ε₁ = 10.5 V, R₁ = 3.50 Ω, R₂ = 5.00 Ω, and R₃ = 4.50 Ω. Given that the current in the lower branch is I₃ = 0.900 A, calculate the electromotive force ε₂ of the lower cell.
items.workedSolution: At junction Q, Kirchhoff's first law gives I₂ = I₁ + I₃. Around the upper loop, ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₂R₂ = 0, so I₁ = (ε₁ − I₃R₂) / (R₁ + R₂) = 0.7059 A and I₂ = 1.606 A. Around the lower loop, ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 12.08 V. Hence the required answer is 12.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's first and second laws to obtain 12.1 V.

items.stem: When a 11.5 Ω load is connected to a mine-rescue cap-lamp battery having ε = 13.4 V and r = 1.9 Ω as illustrated, what is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 13.4 / (11.5 + 1.9) = 1.00 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 13.4 − (1.00)(1.9) = 11.5 V. External load power P = I² R = 11.5 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 11.5 V.

items.stem: An audio preamplifier op-amp has a gain–bandwidth product (GBP) of 1.50 MHz and is configured as a non-inverting amplifier with $R_1 = 4.00\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 96.0\text{ k}\Omega$. Calculate its available closed-loop bandwidth in kHz.
items.workedSolution: Closed-loop gain $G = 1 + \frac{96.0}{4.00} = 25.0$. Using $G \times \mathrm{BW} = \mathrm{GBP}$, $\mathrm{BW} = \frac{1.50 \times 10^6}{25.0} = 60\,000\text{ Hz} = 60.0 kHz$.

markScheme.criterion: Available bandwidth equals 60.0 kHz.

items.stem: Why is a silicon photodiode normally operated in reverse-biased photoconductive mode in optical receivers, and how is it adapted to detect atomic/ionising particles?
items.workedSolution: Reverse bias widens the depletion region for fast response: reverse-biased photodiode current is proportional to light intensity and pairs with a scintillator for particle detection.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that reverse-biased photodiode current is proportional to light intensity and pairs with a scintillator for particle detection.

options.label: A
options.text: A reverse-biased photodiode current is proportional to light intensity and pairs with a scintillator for particle detection that converts incoming nuclear particle energy into visible light flashes.

options.label: B
options.text: Forward bias maximizes reverse dark resistance while direct alpha impacts shatter the diode into a speaker.
options.distractorRationale: Forward bias produces large exponential conduction swamping the tiny photocurrent.

options.label: C
options.text: Reverse bias ensures photocurrent is strictly independent of light intensity across all wavelengths.
options.distractorRationale: In photoconductive mode reverse photocurrent scales linearly with light intensity.

options.label: D
options.text: Silicon photodiodes detect atomic particles purely by measuring their magnetic field like a Hall probe.
options.distractorRationale: They detect light flashes emitted by a coupled scintillator crystal.

items.stem: Why is a Schmitt-trigger NOT gate used instead of a standard single-threshold NOT gate to square up a slowly varying, noisy sensor waveform?
items.workedSolution: Because separate upper and lower switching thresholds provide hysteresis preventing noisy input signals from causing false switching, the output switches cleanly without multiple chatter transitions.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that separate upper and lower switching thresholds provide hysteresis preventing noisy input signals from causing false switching.

options.text: Schmitt trigger removes the DC component of the sensor signal using an internal transformer.
options.distractorRationale: A Schmitt trigger is a DC-coupled logic gate using voltage hysteresis.

options.label: B
options.text: Schmitt trigger amplifies small noise ripples linearly around a single midpoint voltage.
options.distractorRationale: A single midpoint causes chatter; hysteresis prevents chatter.

options.label: C
options.text: Schmitt trigger slows down output rise times so digital counters cannot trigger.
options.distractorRationale: A Schmitt trigger produces crisp, fast logic transitions.

options.label: D

items.stem: Two ideal cells of emfs ε₁ = 1.50 V and ε₂ = 6.00 V are wired in opposing polarity in the two-resistor polarity loop shown, together with R₁ = 4.50 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. The ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 2.70 V. The circuit remains closed for 5 min.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing emfs (ε_net = 4.50 V) and evaluates I = V₁ / R₁ = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Correct resistance R₂ = 3.00 × 10³ Ω.
Converts 5 min to 300 s and applies E = V₁²t / R₁ (or IV₁t).
Correct thermal energy dissipated 0.486 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the circuit current and hence determine the resistance of R₂.
workingSteps: Opposing cells give net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.500 V.
Series current I = V₁ / R₁ = 2.7 / 4500 = 6.000 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Potential difference V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.800 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 3.000 × 10³ Ω ≈ 3.00 × 10³ Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy dissipated in resistor R₁ during the 5 min interval.

items.stem: A hydrazine-line warming element uses a battery of emf 73.2 V and internal resistance 1.9 Ω wired across a 22.5 Ω heating load, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the 22.5 Ω load during 75 s?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 73.2 / (22.5 + 1.9) = 3.00 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 67.5 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 1.52 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 3.00 A and E_ext = I² R t = 1.52 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: A single-loop micro-hydro battery buffer circuit combines opposing sources (12 V with 0.6 Ω, and 8 V with 1.7 Ω; depicted as net ε and r) in series with 5 Ω and 6 Ω resistive elements. What steady current circulates around the loop?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 12 − 8 = 4 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 0.6 + 1.7 + 5 + 6 = 13.3 Ω. Loop current I = 4 / 13.3 = 0.301 A. Load p.d. V = 1.80 V and load power P = 0.543 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 0.301 A.

items.stem: A student calculates a mean wire diameter of 0.3426 mm with an absolute uncertainty of ±0.0084 mm. Following AQA PS 3.3 / MS 1.1 conventions, how should the value and uncertainty be rounded?
items.workedSolution: ±0.0084 mm rounds to ±0.008 mm (3 decimal places), so the mean 0.3426 mm is rounded to 3 decimal places: 0.343 ± 0.008 mm. Therefore the correct statement is: To report precision consistently, round the absolute uncertainty to one significant figure and quote the measured mean value to the exact same decimal place as that uncertainty (giving 0.343 ± 0.008 mm).

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: round the absolute uncertainty to one significant figure and quote the measured mean value to the exact same decimal place as that uncertainty.

options.label: A
options.text: Always keep four significant figures in both the mean value and the uncertainty so zero calculator information is lost (0.3426 ± 0.0084 mm).
options.distractorRationale: Quoting unrounded calculator digits beyond the uncertain decimal place implies false precision.

options.label: B
options.text: Round both the mean value and the absolute uncertainty independently to one significant figure (0.3 ± 0.008 mm).
options.distractorRationale: Only the absolute uncertainty is rounded to 1 s.f. (or 2 s.f. if leading digit is 1); the mean value is matched to the same *decimal place*, not 1 s.f.

options.label: C
options.text: To report precision consistently, round the absolute uncertainty to one significant figure and quote the measured mean value to the exact same decimal place as that uncertainty (giving 0.343 ± 0.008 mm).

options.label: D
options.text: Match the number of significant figures of the mean value to the uncertainty regardless of decimal places.
options.distractorRationale: Value and absolute uncertainty must align in *decimal places*, not significant figure counts.

items.stem: During Required Practical 9, a capacitor discharges through a 100 kΩ resistor. The $\ln(V / \mathrm{V})$ against $t$ graph passes through $(15\text{ s}, 2.030)$ and $(75\text{ s}, 0.212)$. Determine the capacitance $C$ in μF.
items.workedSolution: Ideal time constant $\tau = RC = 33.0 s$, $C = 330$ μF, $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2 = 22.9 s$, and with parallel voltmeter $R_{\mathrm{eff}} = R R_V / (R + R_V)$, $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}} = 27.5 s$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines capacitanceUF $= 330 μF$.

items.stem: Refer to the series test loop for a marine deep-cycle cell load-bank test: increasing current drawn from 1.4 A to 3.4 A reduces terminal voltage from 13.8 V to 7.8 V. What is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (13.8 − 7.8)/(3.4 − 1.4) = 3.00 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 13.8 + (1.4)(3.00) = 18.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 3.00 Ω.

items.stem: Within a joystick goniometer divider with load resistor, a 168 Ω load bridges the 56 Ω resistor of a series divider completed by a 16 Ω resistor across an ideal 29 V rail. What loaded output potential difference appears across the 168 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (56 × 168)/(56 + 168) = 42.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 29 × 42.0 / (16 + 42.0) = 21.0 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 168 = 0.125 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 168 = 2.63 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (42.0 Ω) to obtain 21.0 V.

items.stem: The diagram shows a scaling resistor array built from resistors whose values are multiples of R between terminals P and Q. The top branch contains 3R, and the lower branch consists of R in series with the parallel pair (6R || 12R) and another R. What is the total resistance between P and Q in terms of R?
items.workedSolution: Inner parallel pair: (6R × 12R) / (6R + 12R) = 4R. Lower branch total: R + 4R + R = 6R. Combining in parallel with 3R gives R_PQ = (3 × 6) / (3 + 6) R = 2R.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces the inner parallel pair, series lower branch, and outer parallel combination to obtain 2R.

items.stem: Two identical ideal cells, each of emf 6.00 V, are connected in parallel to drive a 15.0 Ω load in a weather-station battery bank. What reading is shown on the ideal ammeter A in the main branch?
items.workedSolution: Identical ideal cells in parallel maintain terminal pd V = ε = 6.00 V (not 2ε). Main-branch current I = ε / R = 0.4000 A, and each cell supplies I/2 = 0.2000 A. Thus the answer is 0.400 A.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = ε for parallel identical cells to obtain 0.400 A.

items.stem: Which description accurately characterises the current–voltage behaviour of the silicon semiconductor diode plotted in the graph?
items.workedSolution: A diode conducts sharply above forward threshold potential difference (~0.6–0.7 V) with decreasing (non-zero) resistance, and has very high resistance in reverse bias. Therefore option B is correct: conducts sharply above forward threshold potential difference with decreasing resistance while reverse bias has very high resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: conducts sharply above forward threshold potential difference with decreasing resistance while reverse bias has very high resistance.

options.distractorRationale: Describes an ohmic resistor, not an asymmetric diode.

options.text: A semiconductor diode conducts freely in reverse bias and blocks current in forward bias
options.distractorRationale: Reverses forward and reverse bias polarity.

items.stem: Comparing the solid (higher Q) and dashed (lower Q) response curves for an AM radio receiver front-end, what trade-off governs choosing a very high Q factor?
items.workedSolution: Because $f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$, a higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.

options.label: A
options.text: Higher Q factor gives sharper selectivity rejecting adjacent stations but narrows bandwidth so outer sidebands may be attenuated.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher Q factor widens bandwidth, admitting adjacent stations while improving bass audio.
options.distractorRationale: Higher Q narrows bandwidth ($f_{\mathrm{B}} = f_0/Q$).

options.label: C
options.text: Lower Q factor gives sharper selectivity so closely spaced transmitters never overlap.
options.distractorRationale: Lower Q gives a broad curve with poor selectivity.

options.label: D
options.text: Changing Q factor shifts the resonant carrier frequency $f_0$ upward without altering peak sharpness.
options.distractorRationale: $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ is set by $L$ and $C$; Q sets sharpness and bandwidth.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a six-cell series cartridge. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.450 A, V₁ = 7.77 V) and (I₂ = 1.45 A, V₂ = 6.37 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.500 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 26.0 mV when it carries 1.80 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 3.00 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 1.400 Ω ≈ 1.40 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 8.400 V ≈ 8.40 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01444 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.878 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.88 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0867 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 1.40 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 8.40 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0144 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.88 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0867 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 7.77 + 0.45 × 1.400 Ω = 8.400 V ≈ 8.40 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02600 V / 1.800 A = 0.01444 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: An automated greenhouse cooling fan is controlled by a three-stage electronic circuit: (1) a reverse-biased Zener diode voltage reference and thermistor divider, (2) an op-amp comparator, and (3) an N-channel enhancement MOSFET switching the 12 V DC fan motor with a parallel diode.
items.workedSolution: A zener diode sets a stable reference potential comparator compares sensor voltage and mosfet switches high load current without loading the op-amp. Reverse Zener breakdown holds the reference voltage steady, the comparator gives sharp saturated switching, the insulated-gate MOSFET carries high drain current once $V_{\mathrm{GS}} > V_{\mathrm{th}}$, and the parallel flyback diode clamps inductive turn-off spikes.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that the reverse-biased Zener diode operates in breakdown to provide a stable reference voltage independent of supply variations.
Explains how the sensor divider supplies a varying input voltage compared against the reference.
Explains that the op-amp comparator switches sharply to saturation when the threshold temperature is crossed.
States that the MOSFET turns ON when $V_{\mathrm{GS}} > V_{\mathrm{th}}$ to handle high motor load current.
Explains that the MOSFET's insulated gate provides virtually infinite input resistance so negligible current is drawn from the op-amp.
Explains that the reverse-biased protection diode across the inductive motor safely conducts induced back-emf current at turn-off.

parts.prompt: Explain the role of each stage in the circuit and the key electrical properties of the Zener diode, comparator, MOSFET, and parallel protection diode that allow reliable automatic fan operation.
parts.expectedAnswer: In this three-stage controller, a zener diode sets a stable reference potential comparator compares sensor voltage and mosfet switches high load current without loading the op-amp. Specifically, the reverse-biased Zener diode operates in breakdown to hold the reference input steady even if the battery supply fluctuates, while the thermistor divider produces a temperature-dependent voltage. The open-loop op-amp comparator drives its output sharply to positive saturation whenever the temperature voltage exceeds the reference, avoiding half-on linear dissipation in the switch. Because the enhancement MOSFET has an insulated silicon dioxide gate with virtually infinite input resistance, it draws negligible gate current from the op-amp and switches ON sharply once gate-source voltage exceeds threshold to supply high drain current to the fan; finally, the reverse-biased flyback diode across the inductive motor provides a safe path for induced current when switching OFF, protecting the MOSFET from high-voltage back-emf spikes.
workingSteps: L1: Identify Stage 1 (Zener voltage reference + sensor divider), Stage 2 (op-amp comparator), and Stage 3 (MOSFET switch + protection diode).
L1: State that the Zener diode is reverse-biased in breakdown to keep the reference voltage constant despite supply drift.
L2: Explain that the op-amp comparator switches rapidly between saturation rails when $V_+ > V_-$ so the MOSFET switches cleanly.
L2: Explain that the MOSFET conducts large motor current once $V_{\mathrm{GS}} > V_{\mathrm{th}}$.
L3: Highlight that the insulated gate gives ultra-high input resistance so the MOSFET does not load the op-amp output.
L3: Explain the reverse-biased flyback diode safely dissipating inductive back-emf current at turn-off to protect the MOSFET.

items.stem: During steady-state calibration of a wind-turbine gearbox oil-temperature probe, an ideal 5 V cell drives a 160 Ω resistor in series with a 260 Ω NTC thermistor (whose resistance falls with increasing temperature). What potential difference appears across the 260 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 160 + 260 = 420 Ω. Current I = 5 / 420 = 0.0119 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 5 × 260 / 420 = 3.10 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0368 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 3.10 V.

items.stem: In a radiation-detector HV bleed divider, a non-ideal moving-coil ammeter of coil resistance 3.2 Ω (modelled as the 3.2 Ω series element) sits in the main line of an ideal 10 V source feeding parallel 9 Ω and 18 Ω resistors. What current does the ammeter register?
items.workedSolution: Parallel load R_p = (9 × 18)/(9 + 18) = 6.00 Ω. Including the non-ideal ammeter resistance 3.2 Ω gives R_tot = 3.2 + 6.00 = 9.20 Ω, so I = 10 / 9.20 = 1.09 A.

markScheme.criterion: Includes ammeter coil resistance 3.2 Ω in series with R_p = 6.00 Ω to obtain 1.09 A.

items.stem: A three-channel audio mixer uses a summing op-amp ($\pm 12.0\text{ V}$ saturation) with $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 60\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_1 = 15\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_2 = 30\text{ k}\Omega$, and $R_3 = 60\text{ k}\Omega$. When $V_1 = +1.20\text{ V}$, $V_2 = +1.80\text{ V}$, and $V_3 = -0.60\text{ V}$, calculate $V_{\mathrm{out}}$.
items.workedSolution: Using virtual-earth KCL: $V_{\mathrm{out}} = -R_{\mathrm{f}}\left(\frac{V_1}{R_1} + \frac{V_2}{R_2} + \frac{V_3}{R_3}\right) = -60\left(\frac{1.20}{15} + \frac{1.80}{30} + \frac{-0.60}{60}\right) = -60(0.08 + 0.06 - 0.01) = −7.80 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Summing amplifier output equals −7.80 V.

items.stem: In the cleanroom fan-status monitor shown, ideal ammeter A measures the main current leaving an ideal 29 V cell before a junction splits into a 12 Ω + 7 Ω series arm and a parallel 27 Ω arm. What reading appears on ammeter A?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 12 + 7 = 19 Ω, so I_1 = 29 / 19 = 1.53 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 29 / 27 = 1.07 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 2.60 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 1.53 A and 1.07 A to obtain 2.60 A.

items.stem: Within a welding-cable current-diverter rig, current from an ideal 10 V cell traverses a 5 Ω resistor before splitting between cupronickel wire R_1 (5.5 m, 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and a 23 Ω shunt. What current passes through the cupronickel wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 3.48 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 23)/(R_1 + 23) = 3.03 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 5 + 3.03 = 8.03 Ω; main current I_tot = 1.25 A, V_p = 3.77 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 1.08 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 3.48 Ω and obtains 1.08 A.

items.stem: In the compact dual-cell board shown, both cells have negligible internal resistance, with ε₁ = 8.00 V, R₁ = 2.50 Ω, R₂ = 5.50 Ω, and R₃ = 3.00 Ω. Given that the current in the lower branch is I₃ = 0.700 A, calculate the electromotive force ε₂ of the lower cell.
items.workedSolution: At junction Q, Kirchhoff's first law gives I₂ = I₁ + I₃. Around the upper loop, ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₂R₂ = 0, so I₁ = (ε₁ − I₃R₂) / (R₁ + R₂) = 0.5188 A and I₂ = 1.219 A. Around the lower loop, ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 8.803 V. Hence the required answer is 8.80 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's first and second laws to obtain 8.80 V.

items.stem: Across the terminals of an aviation ELT beacon battery pack (emf 28.64 V, internal resistance 1.9 Ω), a 16 Ω resistor completes a closed loop. What current is delivered by the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 28.64 / (16 + 1.9) = 1.60 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 28.64 − (1.60)(1.9) = 25.6 V. External load power P = I² R = 41.0 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 1.60 A.

items.stem: In an inverting op-amp with its non-inverting pin grounded, why is junction X at the inverting input termed a 'virtual earth'?
items.workedSolution: From $V_{\mathrm{out}} = A_{\mathrm{OL}}(V_+ - V_-)$ with $V_+ = 0$, the inverting input remains very close to zero volts while the op-amp is unsaturated because open-loop gain is very large.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that inverting input remains very close to zero volts while the op-amp is unsaturated because open-loop gain is very large.

items.stem: Why is a Hall effect sensor preferred over a mechanical contact switch in a high-speed engine tachometer?
items.workedSolution: In tachometer systems, a Hall sensor detects passing shaft magnets producing pulses for non-contact speed measurement, remaining immune to dust, oil, and mechanical contact wear.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that Hall sensor detects passing shaft magnets producing pulses for non-contact speed measurement.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: A Hall sensor relies on visible laser beams that work even when covered in opaque oil and grease.
options.distractorRationale: Optical sensors are blocked by grease; Hall sensors detect magnetic fields cleanly through oil or dirt.

options.label: D

options.distractorRationale: Hall sensors respond to magnetic flux density from magnets or ferromagnetic teeth, not radio echoes.

items.stem: In the two-resistor RC astable timing circuit whose waveforms are shown, the mark duration is $t_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.7(R_1 + R_2)C$ and the space duration is $t_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.7 R_2 C$. Why is the mark time $t_{\mathrm{H}}$ always greater than the space time $t_{\mathrm{L}}$?
items.workedSolution: An internal discharge switch connects the junction between $R_1$ and $R_2$ to $0\text{ V}$ during discharge, so the capacitor charges through both resistors in series but discharges only through the lower resistor so mark always exceeds space.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that capacitor charges through both resistors in series but discharges only through the lower resistor so mark always exceeds space.

items.stem: In the dc series polarity circuit shown, two ideal cells of electromotive forces ε₁ = 3.20 V and ε₂ = 8.00 V are connected in opposition in series with R₁ = 2.40 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. An ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 3.00 V. What is the resistance of R₂?
items.workedSolution: Since the positive terminals face each other, net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.800 V. Current I = V₁ / R₁ = 1.250 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across R₂ is V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.800 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 1.440 × 10³ Ω ≈ 1.44 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses opposing net emf ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.80 V to find R₂ = 1.44 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: Refer to a ski-boot insole heater pack illustrated: emf 17.4 V in series with internal resistance 1.3 Ω powers a 4.5 Ω load over 45 s. How much energy reaches the 4.5 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 17.4 / (4.5 + 1.3) = 3.00 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 13.5 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 1.82 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 3.00 A and E_ext = I² R t = 1.82 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Within an UPS battery-pack balancing loop, positive terminals of a 23 V cell (1.6 Ω) and a 9 V cell (1.1 Ω) are joined so their emfs oppose around a single loop (equivalent ε, r shown) containing 7 Ω and 8 Ω resistors. What thermal power is dissipated in the 8 Ω load resistor?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 23 − 9 = 14 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 1.6 + 1.1 + 7 + 8 = 17.7 Ω. Loop current I = 14 / 17.7 = 0.791 A. Load p.d. V = 6.33 V and load power P = 5.00 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 5.00 W.

items.stem: In AQA Required Practical 1 (stationary waves on a string), a student investigates how changing the string's mass per unit length μ affects the first-harmonic frequency f₁ while keeping bridge separation L and suspended tension T fixed. What relationship is observed?
items.workedSolution: With L and T held constant, plotting f₁ against 1/√μ yields a straight line through the origin. Therefore the correct statement is: From f₁ = (1 / 2L) √(T / μ), holding string length and tension constant, increasing the mass per unit length reduces the first-harmonic frequency inversely with the square root of mass per unit length.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: holding string length and tension constant, increasing the mass per unit length reduces the first-harmonic frequency inversely with the square root of mass per unit length.

options.text: Increasing mass per unit length μ increases the first-harmonic frequency proportionally to √μ because heavier strings carry greater momentum.

options.text: Doubling mass per unit length μ halves the first-harmonic frequency because f₁ is inversely proportional to μ.
options.distractorRationale: f₁ is proportional to μ^(−1/2), not μ^(−1), so quadrupling μ halves f₁.

options.label: C
options.text: Changing μ has no effect on the first-harmonic frequency because L sets the wavelength uniquely.
options.distractorRationale: Although λ = 2L stays fixed, wave speed v = √(T/μ) changes, altering f₁ = v/λ.

options.label: D
options.text: From f₁ = (1 / 2L) √(T / μ), holding string length and tension constant, increasing the mass per unit length reduces the first-harmonic frequency inversely with the square root of mass per unit length.

options.label: A
options.text: A low-resistance voltmeter is preferable because it increases the effective resistance and lengthens the time constant.
options.distractorRationale: A parallel voltmeter always reduces net resistance R_eff < R, shortening the apparent time constant.

options.label: B
options.text: Electrolytic capacitors are non-polarised so reversing the terminals only changes the sign of the voltmeter reading.
options.distractorRationale: Reversing polarity on an electrolytic capacitor breaks down the oxide dielectric and can cause venting or rupture.

options.label: C
options.text: Connecting the voltmeter in series with the resistor ensures zero parallel discharge error.
options.distractorRationale: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel; putting a high-R voltmeter in series blocks discharge current.

options.label: D
options.text: Observe electrolytic capacitor polarity and use a very high resistance voltmeter so negligible parallel current discharges the capacitor and lowers the measured time constant.

items.stem: In a Daniel-cell internal-resistance lab, ideal meters across a constant-r source record V_1 = 6.7 V when I_1 = 0.6 A, and V_2 = 4.2 V when I_2 = 2.6 A. What is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (6.7 − 4.2)/(2.6 − 0.6) = 1.25 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 6.7 + (0.6)(1.25) = 7.45 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 1.25 Ω.

items.stem: An ideal 16 V cell powers a throttle-position divider feeding an ECU input where upper resistor 8 Ω feeds the parallel combination of lower divider arm 16 Ω and load 48 Ω. What current flows through the 48 Ω load branch?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (16 × 48)/(16 + 48) = 12.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 16 × 12.0 / (8 + 12.0) = 9.60 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 48 = 0.200 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 48 = 1.92 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (12.0 Ω) to obtain 0.200 A.

items.stem: The diagram shows a symmetric divider ladder built from resistors whose values are multiples of R between terminals P and Q. The top branch contains 3R, and the lower branch consists of R in series with the parallel pair (2R || 2R) and another R. What is the total resistance between P and Q in terms of R?
items.workedSolution: Inner parallel pair: (2R × 2R) / (2R + 2R) = 1R. Lower branch total: R + 1R + R = 3R. Combining in parallel with 3R gives R_PQ = (3 × 3) / (3 + 3) R = 1.5R.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces the inner parallel pair, series lower branch, and outer parallel combination to obtain 1.5R.

items.stem: Within a poultry-house lighting relay, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 20 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (120 kΩ in darkness; 1 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 12 V supply. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 120 + 20 = 140 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 140000 = 8.57 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 1.71 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 20 / (1 + 20) = 11.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 8.57 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: An ideal 7 V cell drives a resistance-thermometer bridge arm made of a 18 Ω resistor in series with cupronickel wire R_1 (length 3.6 m, area 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m², resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m). What current flows through the series circuit?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m)(3.6) / (4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 3.04 Ω. Series current I = 7 / (18 + 3.04) = 0.333 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 1.01 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 3.04 Ω and obtains 0.333 A.

items.stem: While bench-testing a dual-zone incubator heating stage, an engineer wires a 10 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 18 Ω and 36 Ω resistors across an ideal 26.4 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 18 Ω and 36 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (18 × 36)/(18 + 36) = 12.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 26.4 × 12.0 / (10 + 12.0) = 14.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 12.0 Ω and finds V_p = 14.4 V.

items.stem: Two identical ideal cells, each of emf 7.50 V, are connected in parallel across a 25.0 Ω resistor in a bench demonstration board, as shown. What is the steady current supplied by each individual cell?
items.workedSolution: Identical ideal cells in parallel maintain terminal pd V = ε = 7.50 V (not 2ε). Main-branch current I = ε / R = 0.3000 A, and each cell supplies I/2 = 0.1500 A. Thus the answer is 0.150 A.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = ε for parallel identical cells to obtain 0.150 A.

items.stem: How must a student determine the electrical resistance $R$ of a non-ohmic filament lamp at point P on its curved $I\text{–}V$ characteristic graph?
items.workedSolution: Resistance is defined strictly as $R = V/I$ at the operating point and never one over the tangent gradient. Therefore option C is correct: divide potential difference by current at the operating point and never take one over the tangent gradient.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: divide potential difference by current at the operating point and never take one over the tangent gradient.

items.stem: When reading the bandwidth $f_{\mathrm{B}}$ of a parallel LC tuned circuit from its voltage-against-frequency resonance curve, why is the half-power bandwidth defined using the factor $0.707$ rather than $0.5$?
items.workedSolution: Because signal power $P \propto V^2$, half the peak power occurs when $V = V_{\max}/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707 V_{\max}$; hence bandwidth is measured between the frequencies where output voltage drops to 0.707 of maximum.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that bandwidth is measured between the frequencies where output voltage drops to 0.707 of maximum.

options.label: A
options.text: Bandwidth is measured at half the peak voltage because output power is directly proportional to voltage.
options.distractorRationale: Power dissipated in a load is proportional to $V^2$, so half-power occurs at $V_{\max}/\sqrt{2} = 0.707 V_{\max}$.

options.label: B
options.text: Bandwidth is measured at the zero-voltage baseline where inductive and capacitive reactances vanish.
options.distractorRationale: The resonance curve approaches zero asymptotically; bandwidth uses the half-power ($-3\text{ dB}$) points.

options.label: C
options.text: Bandwidth is measured at $0.37 V_{\max}$ to match the exponential decay constant of an RC circuit.
options.distractorRationale: $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$ applies to RC time constants, not AC resonance half-power bandwidth.

options.label: D
options.text: Bandwidth is measured between the frequencies where output voltage drops to 0.707 of maximum.

items.stem: An arctic lidar heater-and-blower battery bus connects parallel 9 Ω and 18 Ω loads via a 2 Ω series resistor to a 15 V cell of internal resistance 2 Ω. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 30 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (9 × 18)/(9 + 18) = 6.00 Ω, R_ext = 2 + 6.00 = 8.00 Ω, and R_tot = 8.00 + 2 = 10.0 Ω. Current I = 15 / 10.0 = 1.50 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 15 − (1.50)(2) = 12.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 540 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 540 J.

items.stem: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the electromotive force ε and internal resistance r of a portable telemetry battery. In part (a), two reliable pairs of readings recorded on the ideal ammeter and voltmeter are (I₁ = 0.500 A, V₁ = 6.65 V) and (I₂ = 1.70 A, V₂ = 5.33 V). In part (b), to assess systematic lead errors, the student tests a 0.550 m sample of the connecting wire (cross-sectional area 8.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) and measures a potential difference of 28.0 mV when it carries 2.20 A. The complete experimental circuit uses a total connecting-wire length of 2.75 m.
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating. (a)(ii) straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force. (a)(iii) r = (V₁ − V₂)/(I₂ − I₁) = 1.100 Ω ≈ 1.10 Ω. (a)(iv) ε = V₁ + I₁r = 7.200 V ≈ 7.20 V. (b)(i) R_w = 0.01273 Ω, so ρ = R_w A_w / L_w = 1.967 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m ≈ 1.97 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. (b)(ii) Total lead resistance is 0.0636 Ω, giving a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.

markScheme.criterion: Adjusts variable resistor to take multiple pairs of ammeter (I) and voltmeter (V) readings across a wide range.
Opens switch S between readings (or avoids excessive currents) to prevent heating / cell discharge.
States a straight line of negative gradient equal to −r.
States the vertical-axis intercept (at I = 0) equals the electromotive force ε.
Applies r = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁) correctly with the two given data pairs.
Correct internal resistance r = 1.10 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + Ir to obtain ε = 7.20 V.
Computes R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.0127 Ω (converting mV to V) and substitutes into ρ = R_w A_w / L_w.
Correct wire resistivity 1.97 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
States negligible effect on ε (lead resistance 0.0636 Ω ≪ r, and at I = 0 intercept lead pd drop is zero).

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental procedure used to obtain a suitable set of (I, V) readings with this circuit, including one precaution to reduce error.
parts.expectedAnswer: To collect reliable data, adjust the variable resistor to obtain a range of ammeter and voltmeter readings and open the switch between readings to minimise cell heating.
workingSteps: Vary the variable resistor across its working range and record corresponding pairs of ammeter and voltmeter readings in a table.
Close the momentary switch only while taking each reading so the cell does not heat up or run down.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape and key graphical features of the graph obtained when terminal potential difference V (vertical axis) is plotted against current I (horizontal axis).
parts.expectedAnswer: The V against I graph is a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the internal resistance and a vertical intercept equal to the electromotive force.
workingSteps: Compare the circuit equation with the linear graph form linking terminal potential difference and current.
Identify the vertical intercept as the electromotive force and the negative gradient as minus the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: Use the two measured pairs of (I, V) readings to calculate the internal resistance r of the cell.
workingSteps: From V = ε − Ir, internal resistance r = −ΔV / ΔI = (V₁ − V₂) / (I₂ − I₁).

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the electromotive force ε of the cell.
workingSteps: Substitute into ε = V₁ + I₁r = 6.65 + 0.5 × 1.100 Ω = 7.200 V ≈ 7.20 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the connecting wire material from the sample test data.
workingSteps: Sample wire resistance R_w = V_w / I_w = 0.02800 V / 2.200 A = 0.01273 Ω.

parts.prompt: State and explain whether the total length of connecting wire significantly affects the measured value of ε.
parts.expectedAnswer: The connecting wire has a negligible effect on the measured electromotive force because the lead resistance is very small and produces zero potential drop at zero current.
workingSteps: Compare total connecting-lead resistance with internal resistance and consider the zero-current vertical intercept.

items.stem: A reverse-biased 5.6 V Zener diode provides a reference voltage to a high-resistance op-amp comparator input (drawing negligible current) from a 12.0 V DC supply. The Zener diode requires a minimum reverse current of 10.0 mA to remain cleanly on the steep breakdown region of its $I$–$V$ characteristic. Calculate the maximum permissible value of the series current-limiting resistor $R_{\mathrm{s}}$.
items.workedSolution: Because the comparator input draws negligible current, the series resistor carries $I_{\mathrm{Z,min}} = 10.0\text{ mA}$ with potential difference $V_{\mathrm{s}} - V_{\mathrm{Z}} = 12.0 - 5.6 = 6.4\text{ V}$, giving $R_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{6.4}{10.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 640 Ω$.

markScheme.criterion: Series current-limiting resistor equals 640 Ω.

items.stem: In the induction-cooktop pan-temperature sensor diagram, R_1 is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) wired in series with a 480 Ω precision resistor across an ideal 7 V supply. At an operating point where the p.d. across R_1 is 3.00 V, calculate R_1.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 480 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 7 − 3.00 = 4.00 V. Current I = 4.00 / 480 = 8.33 × 10⁻³ A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 3.00 / 8.33 × 10⁻³ = 360 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 4.00 V to find I = 8.33 × 10⁻³ A and R_1 = 360 Ω.

items.stem: A 4.65 m cylindrical manganin wire of diameter 0.76 mm and resistivity 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m acts as load R_1 inside a camera-lens anti-fog heater ring energised at 12 V (ideal). What thermal power is dissipated in R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.76 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 4.54 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 4.92 Ω. Current I = 12 / 4.92 = 2.44 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 29.3 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 29.3 W.

items.stem: An ideal 15 V rail energises an industrial PLC input-impedance check with 130 Ω and 200 Ω series resistors; probing across 200 Ω with a 300 Ω finite-impedance voltmeter (shown in parallel) produces what reading?
items.workedSolution: The 300 Ω voltmeter shunts the 200 Ω resistor: R_p = (200 × 300)/(200 + 300) = 120 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 15 × 120 / (130 + 120) = 7.20 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 200 Ω and 300 Ω in parallel (120 Ω) to obtain V = 7.20 V.

items.stem: A strain-gauge bridge feeds a balanced difference amplifier ($R_1 = 6.00\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_{\mathrm{f}} = 120\text{ k}\Omega$, rails $\pm 12.0\text{ V}$) with $V_- = 2.42\text{ V}$ on the inverting path and $V_+ = 2.77\text{ V}$ on the non-inverting path. Calculate $V_{\mathrm{out}}$.
items.workedSolution: For matched resistor pairs, $V_{\mathrm{out}} = (V_+ - V_-)\frac{R_{\mathrm{f}}}{R_1} = (2.77 - 2.42)\frac{120}{6.00} = 0.35 \times 20 = 7.00 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Difference amplifier output equals 7.00 V.

items.stem: Three resistors of 15 Ω, 10 Ω, and 6 Ω are wired in parallel inside an automated packaging-line sensor bus and fed through a 12 Ω resistor from an ideal 45 V DC source. What current flows through the 15 Ω branch?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/15 + 1/10 + 1/6, giving R_p = 3.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 12 + 3.00 = 15.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 45 / 15.0 = 3.00 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 9.00 V, and I(15 Ω) = V_p / 15 = 0.600 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 0.600 A.

items.stem: The aircraft pitot-tube dual-path de-icer schematic shows an ideal 30 V supply driving a 8 Ω resistor in series with the parallel pair of titanium wire R_1 (L = 2.5 m, A = 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and 18 Ω. What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 18 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 3.50 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 18)/(R_1 + 18) = 2.93 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 8 + 2.93 = 10.9 Ω; main current I_tot = 2.74 A, V_p = 8.04 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 2.30 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 3.50 Ω and obtains 2.93 Ω.

items.stem: The diagram shows a sensor bias circuit containing two cells of negligible internal resistance. In the upper branch ε₁ = 14.0 V and R₁ = 6.00 Ω; in the shared middle branch R₂ = 4.00 Ω; and in the bottom branch R₃ = 7.00 Ω carries a current I₃ = 1.20 A. What is the current I₁ in the upper branch?
items.workedSolution: At junction Q, Kirchhoff's first law gives I₂ = I₁ + I₃. Around the upper loop, ε₁ − I₁R₁ − I₂R₂ = 0, so I₁ = (ε₁ − I₃R₂) / (R₁ + R₂) = 0.9200 A and I₂ = 2.120 A. Around the lower loop, ε₂ = I₂R₂ + I₃R₃ = 16.88 V. Hence the required answer is 0.920 A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's first and second laws to obtain 0.920 A.

items.stem: A seismic field-recorder lead-acid cell of emf 10.4 V and internal resistance 1.9 Ω is wired directly across a 8.5 Ω external resistor, as shown. What power is dissipated in the 8.5 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 10.4 / (8.5 + 1.9) = 1.00 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 10.4 − (1.00)(1.9) = 8.50 V. External load power P = I² R = 8.50 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 8.50 W.

items.stem: Which set of characteristics accurately defines an ideal operational amplifier?
items.workedSolution: An ideal operational amplifier has infinite open-loop voltage gain infinite input resistance and zero output resistance (plus infinite bandwidth).

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that infinite open-loop voltage gain infinite input resistance and zero output resistance.

items.stem: From the simplified structure of an N-channel enhancement MOSFET, why does its gate draw virtually zero steady current and why does drain current remain zero until $V_{\text{GS}} > V_{\text{th}}$?
items.workedSolution: In an N-channel enhancement MOSFET, the insulated oxide gate over p-substrate gives very high input resistance and conduction above Vth.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that insulated oxide gate over p-substrate gives very high input resistance and conduction above Vth.

options.label: A
options.text: The gate is soldered directly to the source via a copper bridge so current bypasses the substrate.
options.distractorRationale: An insulating silicon dioxide layer isolates the gate electrode completely from the semiconductor.

options.label: B
options.text: Drain current flows continuously at $V_{\text{GS}} = 0\text{ V}$ and is switched off only when $V_{\text{GS}}$ exceeds $V_{\text{th}}$.
options.distractorRationale: An ENHANCEMENT MOSFET is normally OFF at $V_{\text{GS}} = 0\text{ V}$ and conducts only when $V_{\text{GS}} > V_{\text{th}}$.

options.label: C
options.text: The gate requires a large base current to inject minority holes into the silicon dioxide layer.
options.distractorRationale: Large base current applies to bipolar junction transistors (BJTs), not voltage-controlled MOSFETs.

options.label: D

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that produces a single output pulse of fixed duration determined by R and C after each trigger.

items.stem: In the kilohm series test loop shown, two ideal cells of electromotive forces ε₁ = 2.40 V and ε₂ = 7.20 V are connected in opposition in series with R₁ = 6.00 kΩ and an unknown resistor R₂. An ideal voltmeter across R₁ reads V₁ = 3.20 V. What is the resistance of R₂?
items.workedSolution: Since the positive terminals face each other, net emf ε_net = ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.800 V. Current I = V₁ / R₁ = 5.333 × 10⁻⁴ A. Potential difference across R₂ is V₂ = ε_net − V₁ = 1.600 V, so R₂ = V₂ / I = 3.000 × 10³ Ω ≈ 3.00 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses opposing net emf ε₂ − ε₁ = 4.80 V to find R₂ = 3.00 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: Across a 21 Ω element in a diving drysuit heated-vest circuit, a 22 V pack of internal resistance 1 Ω maintains steady current for 75 s. Find the energy converted in the 21 Ω element.
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 22 / (21 + 1) = 1.00 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 21.0 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 1.58 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 1.00 A and E_ext = I² R t = 1.58 × 10³ J.
